docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
One of the most exciting features of the Raspberry Pi 5 is its built-in PCI Express (PCIe) 2.0 x1 connector. By using an M.2 NVMe HAT (Hardware Attached on Top), you can bypass the slow MicroSD card slot and boot your system from a solid-state drive (SSD).

This upgrade boosts read and write speeds from ~40-80 MB/s (on MicroSD) to over 800 MB/s (on NVMe SSD), while eliminating the risk of MicroSD card corruption.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: To follow this guide, you will need: - Raspberry Pi 5 - NVMe M.2 SSD (typically M.2 2230 or 2280 depending on your HAT, M-Key recommended). - M.2 NVMe HAT (e.g., Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+, Pineberry Pi HatDrive, or Waveshare M.2 HAT). - Official Raspberry Pi 27W USB-C Power Supply (highly recommended, as NVMe SSDs draw more power during peak read/write operations).

docs.title: Step 1: Install the Hardware
docs.text:
1. Ensure the Raspberry Pi 5 is completely powered off and unplugged.
  2. Connect the FPC (Flexible Printed Circuit) cable from the NVMe HAT to the Raspberry Pi 5 PCIe port. Be extremely gentle with the ribbon connector lock.
  3. Secure the NVMe HAT onto the Pi 5 using the provided spacers and screws.
  4. Insert your NVMe SSD into the M.2 slot on the HAT and secure it with the mounting screw.

docs.title: Step 2: Flash Raspberry Pi OS to the SSD
docs.text:
The easiest way to install the OS on your SSD is using the Raspberry Pi Imager on another computer.

  1. Connect your NVMe SSD to your PC using a USB-to-NVMe adapter (or mount it to the Pi and use a MicroSD card to run Raspberry Pi Imager locally).
  2. Open Raspberry Pi Imager.
  3. Select Raspberry Pi 5 as the device.
  4. Choose Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit).
  5. Select your NVMe SSD as the target storage.
  6. Click Next and configure any OS settings (like SSH, Username, and Wi-Fi), then write the image.

Alternatively, if you already have the Pi running on a MicroSD card with the SSD connected, you can open the built-in SD Card Copier tool in the Raspberry Pi OS desktop menu to clone your active SD card directly to the SSD.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Boot Priority in EEPROM
docs.text:
For the Raspberry Pi 5 to boot from the PCIe lane instead of looking for a MicroSD card first, you must update the bootloader (EEPROM) settings.

  1. Boot your Pi 5 (using your SD card if the SSD isn't bootable yet).
  2. Open a terminal and edit the bootloader configuration: 
    sudo rpi-eeprom-config --edit
  3. Look for the BOOT_ORDER line. Change it to the following: 
    BOOT_ORDER=0xf416
    Explanation: The number 6 at the end tells the bootloader to try booting from the NVMe device (PCIe) first, before falling back to the SD card (1).
  4. Save and exit the editor (Ctrl+X, Y, Enter).
  5. Reboot your system to apply the bootloader changes: 
    sudo reboot

At this point, you can remove the MicroSD card and verify that the Raspberry Pi 5 boots directly from the SSD.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable PCIe Gen 3 (Speed Override)
docs.text:
By default, the Raspberry Pi 5 PCIe connection is officially rated for PCIe Gen 2.0 speeds (~400-450 MB/s). However, the hardware is capable of running at PCIe Gen 3.0 speeds. While Gen 3 is not officially certified, most modern NVMe SSDs run perfectly fine and double the speed to 800+ MB/s.

  1. Open /boot/firmware/config.txt: 
    sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
  2. Add the following lines to the bottom of the file: 
    # Enable PCIe Gen 3.0 Speeds
dtparam=pciex1_gen=3
  3. Save and close the file.
  4. Reboot the Pi to apply: 
    sudo reboot

docs.title: Step 5: Test the SSD Performance
docs.text:
Once your Pi boots up, open the terminal and measure the read speeds of your SSD to verify PCIe Gen 3 is working.

  1. Install hdparm: 
    sudo apt install hdparm -y
  2. Test the disk read speed (replace /dev/nvme0n1 with your drive identifier if different): 
    sudo hdparm -tT /dev/nvme0n1

docs.title: Expected Results:
docs.text:
• PCIe Gen 2 (Default): Read speeds around 410 - 450 MB/s.
  • PCIe Gen 3 (Enabled): Read speeds around 810 - 870 MB/s!

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The Pi fails to boot from the SSD:
    • Double-check the ribbon FPC cable connection. Unplug and reseat the cable on both the Pi and the HAT.
    • Verify your power supply. Underpowered SSDs will disconnect during boot. If you aren't using the official 27W adapter, the Pi 5 restricts current limits which might crash the SSD.
  • System is unstable at PCIe Gen 3 speeds:
    • Some cheaper NVMe SSDs or poorly shielded FPC cables cannot handle PCIe Gen 3 interference. If you experience random crashes or read/write errors, open /boot/firmware/config.txt and change the parameter to dtparam=pciex1_gen=2 to fall back to the stable Gen 2 standard.

docs.title: How to Build a CI/CD Pipeline for Raspberry Pi with Docker and GitHub Actions
How to Build a CI/CD Pipeline for Raspberry Pi with Docker and GitHub Actions
docs.text:
If you develop applications for your Raspberry Pi (like smart home scripts, web servers, or Discord bots), you have probably faced the tedious workflow of manual deployment: SSHing into the Pi, running git pull, building dependencies, and manually restarting the application.

This manual process is slow and error-prone. A modern CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) pipeline automates this entirely.

In this guide, we will configure a GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runner directly on a Raspberry Pi. We will then build a deployment workflow that triggers on every git push to build a Docker container locally on the Pi and deploy it instantly using Docker Compose.

docs.title: Why Use a Self-Hosted Runner?
docs.text:
GitHub provides free cloud runners to build and run workflows, but they have two major drawbacks for Raspberry Pi deployment: 1. Architecture Mismatch: GitHub's runners run on x86_64 virtual machines. Building ARM-compatible Docker containers on x86 requires emulation (QEMU), which is extremely slow. 2. Firewall Limitations: A standard GitHub cloud runner cannot access a Raspberry Pi sitting behind a home router/firewall without risky configurations like port forwarding.

A Self-Hosted Runner runs locally on your Pi. It connects outbound to GitHub via long-polling (WebSockets), meaning no open ports are needed on your router. Additionally, it builds Docker containers natively on ARM, making builds incredibly fast.

Deployment Flow:
[Push Code] ---> [GitHub Repository]
                        |
            (Outbound Connection / Long-Poll)
                        v
[Raspberry Pi] <--- [Self-Hosted Runner] ---> [Docker Build & Compose Up]

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 running Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit).
  • Docker and Docker Compose installed on your Pi.
  • A GitHub repository hosting your application code.

docs.title: Step 1: Writing the Application Dockerfile
docs.text:
Containerizing your application ensures it runs identically on your development machine and your Raspberry Pi, isolating all dependencies.

Here is an example Dockerfile for a simple Python web server. Save this in the root of your project:

# Use a lightweight official Python image matching the ARM architecture
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Set the working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install system dependencies if needed
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy and install Python requirements
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app runs on
EXPOSE 5000

# Run the application
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

Create a matching docker-compose.yml to manage runtime configuration and automatic restarts:

version: '3.8'

services:
  web-app:
    build: .
    image: local-app:latest
    container_name: my-running-app
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"
    environment:
      - ENV=production

docs.title: Step 2: Setting Up the Self-Hosted Runner on the Pi
docs.text:
Now, we need to register your Raspberry Pi as a runner in your GitHub repository.

  1. On GitHub, go to your repository -> Settings -> Actions -> Runners.
  2. Click New self-hosted runner.
  3. Choose Linux as the runner image and ARM64 as the architecture.
  4. Open a terminal on your Raspberry Pi and run the commands displayed on GitHub. They will look similar to this:
# Create a folder for the runner
mkdir actions-runner && cd actions-runner

# Download the latest runner package
curl -o actions-runner-linux-arm64-2.316.1.tar.gz -L https://github.com/actions/runner/releases/download/v2.316.1/actions-runner-linux-arm64-2.316.1.tar.gz

# Extract the installer
tar xzf ./actions-runner-linux-arm64-2.316.1.tar.gz

docs.title: Configuring the Runner
docs.text:
1. Run the configuration script: 
    ./config.sh --url https://github.com/your-username/your-repo --token YOUR_TOKEN
  2. Follow the prompts: * Enter the runner group name (default is fine). * Name your runner (e.g. pi-deploy-runner). * Add labels. IMPORTANT: Give your runner the label self-hosted and raspberry-pi. This will let you target the Pi specifically in your workflow.

docs.title: Running as a System Service
docs.text:
To prevent the runner from closing when you log out, configure it as a systemd service:

# Install the runner helper service
sudo ./svc.sh install

# Start the runner service
sudo ./svc.sh start

# Verify status
sudo ./svc.sh status

On your GitHub repository settings page, you should now see your runner marked as Idle and Online.

docs.title: Step 3: Creating the GitHub Actions Workflow
docs.text:
With the runner online, we can write the automation instructions. Create a file at .github/workflows/deploy.yml in your repository:

name: CI/CD Deploy to Raspberry Pi

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main # Trigger workflow on pushes to main

jobs:
  deploy:
    name: Build and Deploy Container
    runs-on: [self-hosted, raspberry-pi] # Target your Raspberry Pi runner

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build New Docker Image
        run: |
          docker compose build --no-cache

      - name: Deploy Containers with Docker Compose
        run: |
          docker compose up -d --force-recreate

      - name: Clean Up Stale Docker Images
        run: |
          docker image prune -f

docs.title: Step 4: Testing the Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Ensure you have added the runner user (usually pi or standard login user) to the docker group so the runner can execute docker commands without sudo: 
    sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# Restart the runner service to apply group changes
sudo ./svc.sh stop
sudo ./svc.sh start
  2. Make a change to your application code (e.g., change a text label in your server response).
  3. Commit and push the change to GitHub: 
    git add .
git commit -m "Update UI response text"
git push origin main
  4. Navigate to the Actions tab on your GitHub repository.
  5. Select the running workflow. You will see it connect to your Raspberry Pi, pull the code changes, rebuild the Docker container, and spin up the new version in real-time.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
By running a self-hosted runner natively on the Pi, you avoid cross-compilation errors and enjoy instant, automated local deployment. Every push to your main branch builds, validates, and deploys your changes safely.

This setup is ideal for scaling microservices on a home cluster or ensuring your home automation servers stay up-to-date with minimal downtime.

docs.title: How to Build a Network-Wide Ad Blocker with Raspberry Pi and Pi-hole
How to Build a Network-Wide Ad Blocker with Raspberry Pi and Pi-hole
docs.text:
Tired of seeing invasive ads on your phone, smart TV, computer, and tablet? While browser-based ad blockers like uBlock Origin work well, they only protect the browser they are installed on. They can't block ads inside mobile apps, smart TV streaming applications, or on IoT devices.

Pi-hole is a Linux network-wide software-defined ad blocker that acts as a private Domain Name System (DNS) sinkhole. By routing your home network's DNS queries through a Raspberry Pi running Pi-hole, you can block advertisement and tracking servers before they even reach your devices.

In this guide, we will set up Pi-hole on a Raspberry Pi, configure it as your network's primary DNS server, and integrate Unbound to turn your Pi into a secure, recursive DNS server that resolves domain names directly without relying on upstream providers like Google or Cloudflare.

docs.title: How DNS Sinkholing Works
docs.text:
When you visit a website (e.g., example.com), your device asks a DNS server to translate that domain name into an IP address. 

Without Pi-hole:
[Your Device] ---> (DNS Request: ad.doubleclick.net) ---> [Public DNS] ---> [Ad Server IP] ---> (Ad Loads)

With Pi-hole:
[Your Device] ---> (DNS Request: ad.doubleclick.net) ---> [Pi-hole] ---> [Blocks (returns 0.0.0.0)] ---> (No Ad)

If the requested domain matches a blacklisted advertising server, Pi-hole intercepts the request and returns 0.0.0.0 (nothing). The ad never downloads, saving bandwidth and accelerating page load times.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
Pi-hole is incredibly lightweight. It requires minimal CPU and RAM, meaning you don't need the latest Raspberry Pi model to run it.

  • Any Raspberry Pi: Pi Zero (W / 2 W), Pi 3, Pi 4, or Pi 5.
  • Ethernet Connection (Highly Recommended): Since DNS queries happen constantly, wired Ethernet minimizes latency compared to Wi-Fi.
  • MicroSD Card: 8GB application class (A1/A2) is plenty.
  • Stable Power Supply.

docs.title: Step 1: Set a Static IP on Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text:
Since your Raspberry Pi will act as the DNS server for your entire network, its IP address must not change. If your router assigns a different IP to your Pi after a reboot, your network's internet connection will break.

Before running the installation, configure a static IP on your Pi.

docs.title: For modern Raspberry Pi OS (using NetworkManager):
docs.text:
1. Find your active connection name: 
    nmcli connection show
  2. Set the static IP, gateway, and DNS (replace eth0 with your connection name, and adjust the IP address range for your network): 
    sudo nmcli connection modify "preconfigured" ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns "1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8" ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli connection up "preconfigured"

docs.title: Step 2: Install and Configure Pi-hole
docs.text:
The Pi-hole team provides an interactive shell installer script that automates the deployment process.

  1. Run the installer command: 
    curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash
  2. An installer console wizard will launch. Select OK on the initial informational steps.
  3. Confirm that the installer detected your static IP address correctly.
  4. Choose your Upstream DNS Provider. (e.g., Cloudflare, Google, or OpenDNS. We will change this to our local Unbound server in Step 5).
  5. Choose the default StevenBlack blocklist (containing over 100,000 domains) to begin with.
  6. Enable the Web Admin Interface and choose to install the web server (lighttpd).
  7. Once the setup finishes, the console will display your admin page address and your admin password. Write this down!

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Your Router to Use Pi-hole
docs.text:
To route all home traffic through the Pi-hole, you must configure your router to hand out the Pi-hole's IP address as the primary DNS server via DHCP.

  1. Log into your home router's admin portal (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1).
  2. Locate the DHCP Server settings or LAN settings.
  3. Find the DNS Server fields.
  4. Set Primary DNS to your Raspberry Pi's static IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.100).
  5. Leave the Secondary DNS blank (or set it to 0.0.0.0). Do not set it to a public DNS like Google's 8.8.8.8, as devices will bypass Pi-hole if a secondary is available.
  6. Save settings. Restart the Wi-Fi on your devices to force them to renew their leases and fetch the new DNS configuration.

docs.title: Step 4: Customizing Adlists and Whitelisting
docs.text:
With the router set up, you can access the admin dashboard by visiting: 

http://pi.hole/admin  (or http://<Raspberry_Pi_IP>/admin)

docs.title: Adding Blocklists
docs.text:
While the default list blocks most ads, you can add curated community lists (such as those from The Firebog) to increase efficiency.

  1. Go to Adlists in the left sidebar.
  2. Paste a list URL (e.g., https://v.firebog.net/hosts/AdguardDNS.txt).
  3. Click Add.
  4. Go to Tools -> Gravity and click Update to rebuild the block database.

docs.title: Handling Whitelists
docs.text:
If a site or application breaks (e.g., an email newsletter link containing a tracking redirect is blocked), you can whitelist it:

  1. Go to Query Log.
  2. Locate the blocked domain (marked in red).
  3. Click the green Whitelist button next to it.

docs.title: Step 5: Advanced Optimization (Recursive DNS with Unbound)
docs.text:
Instead of sending your DNS queries to public providers (which track your browsing history), you can install Unbound directly alongside Pi-hole. Unbound is a validating, recursive DNS resolver that queries the authoritative root DNS servers directly.

Query Flow:
[Device] ---> [Pi-hole] ---> [Unbound (Local Recursive DNS)] ---> [Root DNS Servers]

docs.title: Installing Unbound
docs.text:
1. Install the package: 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install unbound -y
  2. Create a configuration file for Pi-hole integration: 
    sudo nano /etc/unbound/unbound.conf.d/pi-hole.conf
  3. Paste the following configuration: 
    server:
    verbosity: 1
    interface: 127.0.0.1
    port: 5335
    do-ip4: yes
    do-udp: yes
    do-tcp: yes

    # May be set to yes if you have IPv6 capability
    do-ip6: no

    # Use this only when you downloaded the list of primary root servers!
    # If for some reason unbound cannot find it, comment this line.
    root-hints: "/var/lib/unbound/root.hints"

    # Trust anchor file, used for DNSSEC validation
    auto-trust-anchor-file: "/var/lib/unbound/root.key"

    # Buffer size adjustments for stability
    so-rcvbuf: 4m
    so-sndbuf: 4m

    # Hide identities
    hide-identity: yes
    hide-version: yes

    # Ensure privacy of local subnets
    private-address: 10.0.0.0/8
    private-address: 172.16.0.0/12
    private-address: 192.168.0.0/16
  4. Restart Unbound: 
    sudo systemctl restart unbound

docs.title: Configuring Pi-hole to Use Unbound
docs.text:
1. Open your Pi-hole Admin Web interface.
  2. Go to Settings -> DNS.
  3. Uncheck all public DNS servers under Upstream DNS Servers.
  4. Under Custom 1 (IPv4), enter: 
    127.0.0.1#5335
  5. Click Save at the bottom.

Your Raspberry Pi is now resolving every domain name recursively, directly communicating with authoritative root servers, validating DNSSEC to prevent cache poisoning, and keeping your queries private.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: With Pi-hole and Unbound running, you have turned your Raspberry Pi into a network shield. You will notice a cleaner web experience, lower data usage, and faster page loads. You can monitor performance via the Dashboard to see what percentage of requests your Pi-hole blocks—often reaching 20-30% on a standard home network!

docs.title: How to Build a Portable Hacking and Security Pentesting Tool with Raspberry Pi and Kali Linux
How to Build a Portable Hacking and Security Pentesting Tool with Raspberry Pi and Kali Linux
docs.text:
In the field of cyber security, testing the defenses of a network (penetration testing) is critical to identifying vulnerabilities before malicious hackers can exploit them.

While dedicated hardware tools like the Flipper Zero or WiFi Pineapple are popular, you can build a far more powerful, flexible, and expandable security diagnostic tool using a Raspberry Pi and Kali Linux.

This guide covers installing Kali Linux on a Raspberry Pi, setting it up for "headless" operation (controlling it from your smartphone or tablet), enabling wireless monitor mode and packet injection, and executing basic security audits using Aircrack-ng and Nmap.

[!CAUTION] Legal Disclaimer: This guide is intended strictly for educational purposes and authorized penetration testing on networks you own or have explicit permission to test. Unauthorized access, interception of data, or disruption of networks is illegal under computer crime laws (e.g., the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in the US).

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
To build a pocket-sized pentesting terminal, you will need:

  • Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5
  • External USB Wi-Fi Adapter: While the Pi's internal Wi-Fi chip is capable, it does not support stable monitor mode or packet injection out-of-the-box. Look for adapters with chipsets like Atheros AR9271 (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA) or Ralink RT5370 which are natively supported by the Linux kernel.
  • Portable Power Bank: A battery pack capable of outputting at least 3A (for Pi 4) or 5A (for Pi 5) to keep the unit running in the field.
  • MicroSD Card (32GB+): Standard Kali installations require significant space for security tool databases.

docs.title: Step 1: Installing Kali Linux on the Pi
docs.text:
Offical ARM images of Kali Linux are tailored specifically for the Raspberry Pi's processor.

  1. Open Raspberry Pi Imager on your computer.
  2. Click Choose OS -> Other specific-purpose OS -> Testing and Security -> Kali Linux.
  3. Select the version matching your Pi model (ensure it is the 64-bit ARM64 release).
  4. Choose your MicroSD card and click Write.
  5. Insert the MicroSD card into your Pi, connect it to your router via Ethernet (for initial setup), and power it on.

The default credentials for Kali Linux are: * Username: kali * Password: kali

docs.title: Step 2: Setting Up Headless Operation via Mobile Device
docs.text:
When using this tool in the field, you won't have a monitor, keyboard, or mouse. Setting up a VNC (Virtual Network Computing) server allows you to control the Pi's graphical desktop directly from a smartphone or tablet.

  1. SSH into your Pi from your laptop: 
    ssh kali@<raspberry-pi-ip>
  2. Update the system: 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
  3. Install and configure TigerVNC: 
    sudo apt install tigervnc-standalone-server -y
vncpasswd
    (Set a secure password when prompted; this is what you will use to connect from your phone).
  4. Create a startup script to launch VNC automatically at boot. Create a systemd service file: 
    sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/vncserver.service
  5. Paste the configuration: 
    [Unit]
Description=Start TigerVNC server at startup
After=syslog.target network.target

[Service]
Type=forking
User=kali
Group=kali
WorkingDirectory=/home/kali
ExecStart=/usr/bin/vncserver -localhost no -geometry 1280x720 :1
ExecStop=/usr/bin/vncserver -kill :1

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
  6. Enable and start the service: 
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable vncserver.service
sudo systemctl start vncserver.service

Now, download a free VNC Viewer app (like RealVNC Viewer) on your phone. Connect to your Pi's IP on port 5901 (e.g., 192.168.1.100:5901) to view and control the Kali desktop natively.

docs.title: Step 3: Enabling Monitor Mode and Packet Injection
docs.text:
To intercept or audit wireless networks, your Wi-Fi card must be switched from Managed Mode (standard client connection) to Monitor Mode (listening to raw radio packets in the air).

  1. Plug in your external USB Wi-Fi adapter.
  2. Identify the interface name (usually wlan1): 
    iwconfig
  3. Kill conflicting network services to prevent them from resetting your card: 
    sudo airmon-ng check kill
  4. Enable monitor mode on your target interface: 
    sudo ip link set wlan1 down
sudo iw dev wlan1 set type monitor
sudo ip link set wlan1 up
  5. Verify the card is now in monitor mode: 
    iwconfig
    The Mode should read Monitor.
  6. Test if your adapter supports packet injection (transmitting custom crafted frames): 
    sudo aireplay-ng --test wlan1
    If successful, you will see a message indicating injection is working and displaying the percentage of packets acknowledged by nearby access points.

docs.title: Step 4: Wireless Security Auditing (Aircrack-ng)
docs.text:
Once monitor mode is active, you can check the security of your home Wi-Fi network by attempting to capture the WPA2 handshake. This handshake occurs when a device connects to your Wi-Fi, exchanging cryptographic keys.

  1. Scan the airwaves to find your home Wi-Fi network's BSSID (MAC address) and channel: 
    sudo airodump-ng wlan1
    Press Ctrl+C once you identify your network. Note the BSSID and Channel (CH).
  2. Begin monitoring and capturing packets on your specific home Wi-Fi channel: 
    sudo airodump-ng -c <channel> --bssid <BSSID> -w WPA_capture wlan1
  3. To capture the handshake immediately, trigger a de-authentication frame to temporarily disconnect your target device (e.g., your test phone). When the phone reconnects automatically, Aircrack will capture the handshake: 
    sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a <BSSID> -c <Client_MAC> wlan1
  4. Once captured, you will see [WPA Handshake: BSSID] appear in the top-right corner of the airodump-ng terminal. You can now stop the capture.
  5. The cryptographic hash is stored in WPA_capture-01.cap. To audit the strength of your password, you can run a dictionary attack locally (or offload it to a faster machine running hashcat): 
    sudo aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt WPA_capture-01.cap

docs.title: Step 5: Network Scanning with Nmap
docs.text:
Once connected to a target test network (either via Wi-Fi or Ethernet), you can map the network topology and identify open ports on host machines.

  1. Perform a fast scan to discover active hosts in your local subnet: 
    nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24
  2. Perform a detailed service version and OS detection scan on a target host IP: 
    sudo nmap -sS -sV -O 192.168.1.50
    * -sS: Stealth TCP SYN scan. * -sV: Standard version detection (identifies what software is running on open ports). * -O: OS detection (guesses the operating system using TCP/IP fingerprinting).

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Your portable pentesting terminal is now complete. By utilizing Kali Linux and an external USB adapter, your Raspberry Pi acts as a fully functional, mobile network security assessment unit. Regularly running auditing tools like Nmap and Aircrack-ng against your own infrastructure is an excellent way to ensure your firewall, encryption standards, and passwords remain secure against modern exploits.

docs.title: How to Build a Private Cloud Storage on Raspberry Pi with Nextcloud
How to Build a Private Cloud Storage on Raspberry Pi with Nextcloud
docs.text:
Commercial cloud storage solutions like Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are incredibly convenient for backing up documents and syncing smartphone photos. However, they come with recurring monthly fees, strict storage limits, and potential privacy concerns regarding where and how your personal data is scanned and stored.

Nextcloud is a powerful, open-source self-hosted productivity platform that serves as a complete alternative to big-tech cloud storage. By running Nextcloud on a Raspberry Pi, you can create your own private cloud storage with no storage caps (limited only by your hard drive size) and total ownership of your files.

In this guide, we will deploy Nextcloud along with a MariaDB database and a Redis cache using Docker Compose on a Raspberry Pi. We will also implement crucial performance optimizations to ensure Nextcloud runs smoothly on the Pi's hardware.

docs.title: Why Use Docker, MariaDB, and Redis?
docs.text:
A manual Nextcloud installation requires configuring Apache/Nginx, PHP, database connectors, and caching services on your host OS. This is tedious and easily breaks during OS upgrades.

Using Docker Compose isolates the services into containers: * Nextcloud (Apache/PHP): The core web application. * MariaDB: An optimized MySQL-compatible database to manage user profiles, file paths, and metadata. * Redis: An in-memory key-value store. This is essential for Raspberry Pi deployments. It handles transactional file locking and session caching, preventing Nextcloud from maxing out the Pi's CPU during file syncs.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
Nextcloud performs database lookups and thumbnail rendering frequently. Standard MicroSD cards are too slow and will wear out quickly.

  • Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5 (Pi 5 is highly recommended for faster page loads).
  • External USB 3.0 SSD: Strongly recommended for database storage and data directories.
  • Wired Ethernet Connection.
  • Official Power Supply.

docs.title: Step 1: Preparing and Mounting External Storage
docs.text:
1. Connect your external SSD to the Pi.
  2. Find the drive's UUID: 
    sudo blkid
  3. Create the mount directory: 
    sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nextcloud-data
  4. Configure auto-mounting on boot by editing /etc/fstab: 
    sudo nano /etc/fstab
  5. Add this line at the end (adjust the UUID and filesystem type to match your drive): 
    UUID=your-ssd-uuid /mnt/nextcloud-data ext4 defaults,noatime,nofail 0 2
  6. Mount the drive and adjust permissions: 
    sudo mount -a
sudo chown -R 33:33 /mnt/nextcloud-data
    Note: 33 is the default UID/GID for the www-data user inside the Nextcloud container. Granting ownership prevents permission denied errors during configuration.

docs.title: Step 2: Creating the Docker Compose Deployment
docs.text:
We will define the Nextcloud, MariaDB, and Redis stack in a single docker-compose.yml file.

  1. Create a project directory: 
    mkdir -p ~/nextcloud && cd ~/nextcloud
  2. Create the composition file: 
    nano docker-compose.yml
  3. Paste the following configuration:
version: '3.8'

services:
  db:
    image: mariadb:10.11
    container_name: nextcloud-db
    command: --transaction-isolation=READ-COMMITTED --binlog-format=ROW
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./db:/var/lib/mysql
    environment:
      - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=your_secure_root_password
      - MYSQL_PASSWORD=your_secure_db_password
      - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
      - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud

  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    container_name: nextcloud-redis
    restart: unless-stopped

  app:
    image: nextcloud:apache
    container_name: nextcloud-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    volumes:
      - ./config:/var/www/html/config
      - ./custom_apps:/var/www/html/custom_apps
      - /mnt/nextcloud-data:/var/www/html/data
    environment:
      - MYSQL_HOST=db
      - MYSQL_DATABASE=nextcloud
      - MYSQL_USER=nextcloud
      - MYSQL_PASSWORD=your_secure_db_password
      - REDIS_HOST=redis
  1. Start the stack: 
    docker compose up -d

It will take a minute for MariaDB to initialize the databases. Once up, access the Nextcloud setup wizard at: 

http://<your-raspberry-pi-ip>:8080

docs.title: Step 3: Web UI Setup
docs.text:
1. Open the Nextcloud setup page in your browser.
  2. Create an admin username and a strong password.
  3. Set the Data Folder to /var/www/html/data (which maps to your external SSD via the Docker volume).
  4. The database configuration will be filled automatically via the environment variables defined in the docker-compose file. Click Install.
  5. Skip or install the recommended apps (Calendar, Contacts, Mail) based on your preference.

docs.title: Step 4: Critical Performance Optimizations for Raspberry Pi
docs.text: Without proper caching and memory configuration, Nextcloud will feel sluggish on Raspberry Pi hardware.

docs.title: 1. Configure Redis for Memory Caching
docs.text:
We need to tell Nextcloud to use our Redis container for caching file locks.

  1. Edit the Nextcloud configuration file: 
    nano ~/nextcloud/config/config.php
  2. Add the Redis configuration block inside the $CONFIG array: 
      'memcache.local' => '\OC\Memcache\APCu',
  'memcache.locking' => '\OC\Memcache\Redis',
  'redis' => [
    'host' => 'redis',
    'port' => 6379,
  ],
  3. Save and exit.

docs.title: 2. Configure Background Jobs (Cron)
docs.text:
By default, Nextcloud processes background maintenance tasks (like cataloging files and generating previews) via "AJAX," meaning every time a user visits the web portal, the Pi executes these tasks. This causes massive load spikes.

Changing this to a system cron ensures tasks run periodically in the background.

  1. Open the Host crontab editor: 
    crontab -e
  2. Add a rule to trigger the Nextcloud internal cron script every 5 minutes inside the running container (replace nextcloud-app with your container name if modified): 
    */5 * * * * docker exec -u 33 nextcloud-app php -f /var/www/html/cron.php
  3. In your Nextcloud Web UI, navigate to Administration Settings -> Basic Settings -> Background jobs, and change the option from AJAX to Cron.

docs.title: Step 5: Mobile Synchronization & Secure Access
docs.text:
To back up your mobile photos automatically:

  1. Download the Nextcloud client app on your Android or iOS device.
  2. Enter your local server URL: http://<your-raspberry-pi-ip>:8080 and log in.
  3. Enable Auto-upload in the app settings to automatically sync newly captured photos and videos to your Pi's external SSD.

docs.title: Secure Remote Access
docs.text: Since you host this locally, the mobile app won't sync when you leave your home Wi-Fi. To access your files securely on the go: * Tailscale: Install the Tailscale Docker container or host package on the Pi. It creates a secure, encrypted wireguard mesh network allowing you to connect using the Pi's Tailscale IP address without port forwarding. * Reverse Proxy + Cloudflare Tunnel: Map a custom domain name (e.g., cloud.yourdomain.com) to your Nextcloud port 8080 using Cloudflare Tunnels for secure HTTPS encryption.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: You now have a fully operational, private cloud storage server running on your Raspberry Pi. Thanks to the SSD storage, Redis locking, and Cron automation, your private cloud is optimized to deliver fast response times while keeping all your sensitive personal data securely under your own roof.

docs.title: How to Build a Raspberry Pi Home Media Server with Plex and Jellyfin
How to Build a Raspberry Pi Home Media Server with Plex and Jellyfin
docs.text:
Commercial streaming services like Netflix, Prime Video, and Spotify are convenient, but they suffer from rising subscription costs, region-locked content, and the risk of titles disappearing overnight.

Building a personal home media server allows you to host, organize, and stream your own collection of movies, TV shows, music, and photos to any device in your house—smart TVs, smartphones, tablets, and computers.

Running this server on a low-power, 24/7-operational Raspberry Pi is the perfect cost-effective solution. In this guide, we will set up the two leading media server platforms, Plex and Jellyfin, on a Raspberry Pi using Docker Compose, configure external USB storage, and optimize performance for local streaming.

docs.title: Plex vs. Jellyfin: Which One Should You Choose?
docs.text:
Before deploying, it helps to understand the difference between the two dominant platforms:

Feature Plex Media Server Jellyfin Media Server License Proprietary (Freemium) Open-Source (100% Free) Hardware Transcoding Requires paid "Plex Pass" subscription Completely Free Mobile Apps Paid unlock fee (without Plex Pass) 100% Free Setup Ease Easiest (handles remote access via accounts) Moderate (requires VPN/Proxy for secure remote access) Privacy Telemetry sent to Plex servers Completely private and self-hosted

Recommendation: If you want a quick setup that works out of the box with polished client apps and don't mind paying for premium features, choose Plex. If you prefer a completely open-source, private, and free system with no paywalls, choose Jellyfin.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
Streaming high-definition video requires decent processing power and fast read speeds.

  • Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5: The Pi 5 is highly recommended if you plan to transcode media.
  • External USB 3.0 Storage: A high-capacity external HDD or SSD to store your media library. Ensure it has an external power supply, as the Pi's USB ports may not provide enough power for large drives.
  • Wired Ethernet Connection: DNS, database lookups, and video streams benefit heavily from low latency and high bandwidth.
  • Official Power Supply.

docs.title: Step 1: Mounting External Storage on Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text:
Since media libraries are large, storing them on the SD card is not viable. We must format and mount an external USB drive.

  1. Connect your external drive to one of the blue USB 3.0 ports on the Pi.
  2. Find the drive identifier (e.g. /dev/sda1): 
    sudo blkid
    Note down the UUID and the TYPE (formatting the drive to ext4 is highly recommended for Linux compatibility).
  3. Create a mount point: 
    sudo mkdir -p /mnt/media
  4. Configure automatic mounting on boot. Edit the fstab file: 
    sudo nano /etc/fstab
  5. Add the following line at the end (replace the UUID with yours): 
    UUID=your-drive-uuid /mnt/media ext4 defaults,noatime,nofail 0 2
  6. Mount the drive: 
    sudo mount -a
  7. Set up the folder structure: 
    sudo mkdir -p /mnt/media/movies /mnt/media/tv /mnt/media/music
sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /mnt/media

docs.title: Step 2: Deploying Jellyfin with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Jellyfin runs perfectly inside Docker containers, keeping configuration separate from your base operating system.

  1. Create a project directory: 
    mkdir -p ~/jellyfin && cd ~/jellyfin
  2. Create a docker-compose.yml file: 
    version: '3.5'
services:
  jellyfin:
    image: jellyfin/jellyfin:latest
    container_name: jellyfin
    network_mode: host
    environment:
      - TZ=Asia/Tokyo # Replace with your timezone
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
      - ./cache:/cache
      - /mnt/media:/media
    restart: unless-stopped
  3. Start the container: 
    docker compose up -d

You can now access your Jellyfin server by navigating to: 

http://<your-raspberry-pi-ip>:8096

docs.title: Step 3: Deploying Plex with Docker Compose
docs.text:
If you decided to go with Plex, here is how to deploy it:

  1. Create a project directory: 
    mkdir -p ~/plex && cd ~/plex
  2. Obtain a claim token by logging into plex.tv/claim. This token links your container to your Plex account.
  3. Create a docker-compose.yml file: 
    version: '3.8'
services:
  plex:
    image: plexinc/pms-docker:latest
    container_name: plex
    network_mode: host
    environment:
      - TZ=Asia/Tokyo # Replace with your timezone
      - PLEX_CLAIM=YOUR_CLAIM_TOKEN # Paste token here
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
      - ./transcode:/transcode
      - /mnt/media:/data
    restart: unless-stopped
  4. Start the container: 
    docker compose up -d

Access the Plex server setup wizard at: 

http://<your-raspberry-pi-ip>:32400/web

docs.title: Step 4: Library Setup and Metadata Scraping
docs.text:
Both servers follow a similar configuration wizard on first launch:

  1. Create Admin Credentials: Set a secure local username and password.
  2. Add Media Library: * Select the library type (e.g. Movies). * Browse to the folder. For Jellyfin, navigate to /media/movies. For Plex, navigate to /data/movies. * Set the preferred language for metadata.
  3. Complete Setup: The server will begin scanning your directories. It automatically matches your filenames against public databases (like TheMovieDB) to fetch movie posters, actor details, synopses, and theme music.

Tip: For accurate metadata scraping, ensure your files are organized correctly, e.g., /media/movies/Avatar (2009)/Avatar (2009).mp4.

docs.title: Step 5: Optimizing Transcoding on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Transcoding is the process where the media server recompresses a video on the fly because the client device (e.g. an older tablet or a phone on a cellular network) cannot play the original file format natively.

Because the Raspberry Pi has an ARM CPU, high-resolution transcoding (especially 4K to 1080p) will heavily overload the processor, leading to buffering and stuttering.

docs.title: 1. Enable Direct Play
docs.text: The best optimization is to avoid transcoding entirely. Configure your clients (Plex or Jellyfin apps) to stream at "Original Quality" or "Maximum Quality" when on the local network. If the client supports the source codec (like H.264 or HEVC), the Pi will stream the file directly without processing it, keeping CPU usage below 5%.

docs.title: 2. Enable Hardware Acceleration (Jellyfin)
docs.text: The Raspberry Pi has hardware video decoders that can offload decoding work. To enable it in Jellyfin: 1. Go to Dashboard -> Playback -> Transcoding. 2. Set Hardware acceleration to Video4Linux2 (V4L2). 3. Scroll down and click Save.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: With your Raspberry Pi media server online, you have a private, self-hosted streaming network. You can download the official Plex or Jellyfin apps on your Smart TV, phone, or tablet, log in, and stream your catalog anywhere in your home. By utilizing containerized deployments and external storage, your system remains robust, modular, and easy to back up.

docs.title: How to Build a Smart Home with Raspberry Pi and Home Assistant
How to Build a Smart Home with Raspberry Pi and Home Assistant
docs.text:
Smart home automation is one of the most practical and exciting projects you can build with a Raspberry Pi. While off-the-shelf commercial hubs like Apple HomeKit, Google Home, or Amazon Alexa are convenient, they often lock you into their ecosystems and send your data to the cloud.

Home Assistant (HA) is a powerful, open-source smart home platform that prioritizes local control and privacy. Running Home Assistant on a Raspberry Pi allows you to unify devices from different manufacturers, run complex automations locally, and keep your data completely inside your home.

This comprehensive guide will walk you through setting up Home Assistant OS (HAOS) on a Raspberry Pi, integrating commercial smart devices, wiring physical GPIO sensors, and setting up automated workflows.

docs.title: Why Raspberry Pi and Home Assistant?
docs.text:
• Local Control: Devices respond instantly because automation logic runs on your local network—no cloud round-trips required.
  • Privacy-First: Your data (when you are home, sensor readings, camera feeds) remains stored locally on your Pi.
  • Massive Compatibility: Home Assistant supports over 2,500 integrations (SwitchBot, Philips Hue, ESPHome, Zigbee, Z-Wave, etc.).
  • GPIO Extensibility: Unlike commercial hubs, you can connect cheap electronics components (like temperature, motion, or light sensors) directly to the Pi's GPIO pins.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
To build a reliable Home Assistant hub, you will need the following hardware:

Component Recommended Specification Why it matters Raspberry Pi Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5 Provides ample CPU and RAM for running multiple add-ons and processing camera feeds. Storage High-End Application Class MicroSD (A2) or SSD Home Assistant writes logs and database entries constantly. Cheap SD cards will corrupt quickly. SSD is highly recommended for long-term stability. Power Supply Official Raspberry Pi Power Supply Prevents under-voltage warnings and database corruption. Sensor (Optional) DHT22 (AM2302) Temperature & Humidity Sensor For hands-on physical sensor integration. Breadboard & Jumpers Female-to-Female jumper wires For connecting the sensor to the GPIO pins.

docs.title: Step 1: Installing Home Assistant OS (HAOS)
docs.text:
Home Assistant OS is a minimal, optimized operating system designed specifically to run Home Assistant. It manages containers, backups, and OS updates automatically via a clean web interface.

  1. Insert your MicroSD card or SSD into your computer.
  2. Open Raspberry Pi Imager.
  3. Click Choose OS -> Other specific-purpose OS -> Home assistants and home automation -> Home Assistant.
  4. Choose the version corresponding to your hardware model (e.g., Home Assistant OS for Raspberry Pi 4 or Pi 5).
  5. Click Choose Storage and select your target drive.
  6. Click Next and write the image.
  7. Once written, insert the storage drive into your Raspberry Pi, connect an Ethernet cable to your router, and power it on.

[!NOTE] The initial boot and installation process can take up to 20 minutes as the Pi downloads the latest Home Assistant containers and sets up the internal database. Do not unplug the power during this phase.

To access your new hub, open a browser on a device connected to the same local network and navigate to: 

http://homeassistant.local:8123
Follow the on-screen prompts to create your owner account and set your location (used for sunrise/sunset automations).

docs.title: Step 2: Integrating Commercial Smart Devices
docs.text:
One of Home Assistant's greatest strengths is its ability to automatically discover smart devices on your local network.

  1. Go to Settings -> Devices & Services.
  2. You will likely see discovered devices (e.g., Google Cast, Apple TV, Philips Hue, ESPHome, or TP-Link Smart Plugs) waiting to be configured.
  3. Click Configure on any detected device and follow the authentication steps.
  4. To add a device manually, click + Add Integration at the bottom right, search for your device brand (such as SwitchBot), and enter the configuration details.

docs.title: Step 3: Connecting a Physical Sensor via GPIO
docs.text: Let's make this a true DIY project by connecting a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor directly to the Raspberry Pi. Home Assistant leverages ESPHome or custom integrations to read GPIO data.

docs.title: Wiring Diagram
docs.text:
Connect the DHT22 sensor to the Raspberry Pi GPIO header as follows:

       DHT22 Sensor                    Raspberry Pi GPIO Pins
     +--------------+                +-------------------------+
     |   1. VCC     |--------------> | Pin 1  (3.3V Power)     |
     |   2. DATA    |--------------> | Pin 11 (GPIO 17)        |
     |   3. NULL    |                |                         |
     |   4. GND     |--------------> | Pin 9  (Ground)         |
     +--------------+                +-------------------------+

docs.title: Reading Sensor Data in Home Assistant
docs.text:
For stability and ease of configuration, using ESPHome (via a cheap $4 ESP8266 or ESP32 micro-controller connected to the Pi via USB or Wi-Fi) is the modern best practice.

However, if you want to read directly from the Pi's own GPIO pins, you can use the Raspberry Pi Remote GPIO custom integration:

  1. Install the Terminal & SSH add-on from the Add-on Store (Settings -> Add-ons).
  2. Open the terminal and edit your config file: 
    nano /config/configuration.yaml
  3. Add the configuration to define the DHT22 sensor on GPIO 17: 
    sensor:
  - platform: dht
    sensor: DHT22
    pin: 17
    name: "Living Room Temp & Humidity"
    monitored_conditions:
      - temperature
      - humidity
  4. Restart Home Assistant (Settings -> System -> Restart). You will now have two new entities: sensor.living_room_temp_humidity_temperature and sensor.living_room_temp_humidity_humidity.

docs.title: Step 4: Creating Smart Automations
docs.text:
Automations in Home Assistant follow a simple structure: Triggers (When...), Conditions (But only if...), and Actions (Then do...).

Let's create an automation that automatically turns on a humidifier (connected to a smart plug) when the living room humidity drops below 40%, but only if someone is home.

docs.title: UI Method
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Settings -> Automations & Scenes -> Create Automation.
  2. Trigger: Click Add Trigger, choose Numeric State, select your humidity sensor entity, and set Below to 40.
  3. Condition: Click Add Condition, choose State, select your tracking entity (e.g., zone.home), and set the state to 1 (or check if a presence sensor is home).
  4. Action: Click Add Action, choose Device, select your Humidifier Smart Plug, and set the action to Turn On.
  5. Click Save and give it a name like "Auto Humidifier ON".

docs.title: YAML Method
docs.text:
If you prefer configuration-as-code, you can write this directly in /config/automations.yaml:

- id: 'auto_humidifier_on'
  alias: Auto Humidifier ON
  trigger:
  - platform: numeric_state
    entity_id: sensor.living_room_temp_humidity_humidity
    below: 40
  condition:
  - condition: state
    entity_id: zone.home
    state: '1'
  action:
  - service: switch.turn_on
    target:
      entity_id: switch.living_room_humidifier_plug
  mode: single

docs.title: Step 5: Secure Remote Access with Tailscale
docs.text:
By default, Home Assistant is only accessible within your home network. To control your home while away, you need a secure remote access solution. Opening ports (port forwarding) on your router is risky. The safest approach is utilizing a Zero Trust mesh VPN like Tailscale.

  1. In Home Assistant, navigate to Settings -> Add-ons -> Add-on Store.
  2. Search for Tailscale and install it.
  3. Start the add-on, open its Web UI, and authenticate with your Tailscale account.
  4. Enable Exit Node or simply use the assigned Tailscale IP address (e.g., 100.x.y.z) to connect securely to http://100.x.y.z:8123 from your phone or laptop anywhere in the world.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Running Home Assistant on your Raspberry Pi shifts the control of your house back into your hands. From here, the possibilities are virtually limitless. You can add Zigbee dongles to connect low-power wireless sensors, integrate local cameras with AI-powered object detection (via Frigate), or build custom dashboards to display on tablets wall-mounted around your home.

By avoiding cloud dependencies, your home remains fast, secure, and fully functional even if your internet connection goes down.

docs.title: How to Build a USB MIDI Device with Raspberry Pi
How to Build a USB MIDI Device with Raspberry Pi
docs.text: Turn your Raspberry Pi into a custom USB MIDI controller or sound module! Using the g_midi kernel module, your Pi will appear as a plug-and-play MIDI device when connected to any Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) or music software.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: USB MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) allows computers and instruments to share musical performance data. By emulating a USB MIDI device with your Raspberry Pi, you can: - Build a hardware MIDI controller using buttons, knobs (potentiometers), and distance sensors. - Receive MIDI notes from a computer DAW (like Ableton Live, FL Studio, or Logic Pro) and trigger hardware solenoids or LED light shows. - Create an on-device hardware synthesizer.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi Model: Pi Zero, Zero W, Zero 2 W, or Raspberry Pi 4 (which support OTG).
  • A USB Data Cable (to connect your Pi to a host computer).
  • Python installed on the Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: Step 1: Enable USB OTG (dwc2)
docs.text:
1. Edit your boot configuration file: 
    sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
  2. Add the dwc2 driver support to the bottom of the file: 
    dtoverlay=dwc2
  3. Save and close.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable the MIDI Gadget Driver
docs.text:
To make the Raspberry Pi boot up as a MIDI device, we need to load the g_midi driver.

  1. Open /etc/modules: 
    sudo nano /etc/modules
  2. Add the following lines to ensure the MIDI module loads at startup: 
    dwc2
g_midi
  3. Optional: Customize the Device Name: By default, your Pi will show up as "MIDI Gadget". You can change this by creating a configuration file for the driver: 
    sudo nano /etc/modprobe.d/g_midi.conf
    Add the following line to define your custom hardware names: 
    options g_midi idVendor=0x1d6b idProduct=0x0104 iManufacturer="MyCompany" iProduct="PiMIDIController"
  4. Reboot your Raspberry Pi: 
    sudo reboot

Once rebooted, connect your Pi to a host computer. The host should automatically recognize a class-compliant USB MIDI device named "PiMIDIController" (or "MIDI Gadget").

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the MIDI Ports
docs.text:
On your Raspberry Pi, you can verify that the MIDI gadget ALSA port is active by listing the midi devices:

amidi -l

You should see an output similar to: 

Dir Device    Name
IO  hw:0,0    f_midi
Here, hw:0,0 is the virtual ALSA port representing the USB connection to the host computer.

docs.title: Step 4: Sending MIDI Signals with Python
docs.text:
To easily handle MIDI messages in Python, we will install the popular mido library and the ALSA back-end package.

  1. Install python packages: 

    sudo apt update
    Install the ALSA development library: 
    sudo apt install libasound2-dev -y
    Install Python mido and python-rtmidi via pip: 
    pip3 install mido python-rtmidi

  2. Write a Python Script to Send Notes: Create a script called midi_send.py that sends a "C4" note-on message, waits one second, and sends a note-off message. 

    import time
import mido

# List available output ports
print("Available ports:", mido.get_output_names())

# Open the virtual USB MIDI port
# Typically named 'f_midi' or 'MIDI Gadget'
try:
    port_name = [name for name in mido.get_output_names() if 'f_midi' in name or 'Gadget' in name][0]
    with mido.open_output(port_name) as outport:
        print(f"Opened port: {port_name}")

        # Send Note On (Middle C, Velocity 64)
        msg_on = mido.Message('note_on', note=60, velocity=64)
        print(f"Sending: {msg_on}")
        outport.send(msg_on)

        time.sleep(1.0)

        # Send Note Off
        msg_off = mido.Message('note_off', note=60, velocity=0)
        print(f"Sending: {msg_off}")
        outport.send(msg_off)

except IndexError:
    print("Error: Could not find USB MIDI output port. Is g_midi loaded?")

  3. Run the Script: 

    python3 midi_send.py

Open any software synth or DAW (like GarageBand, Ableton, or a web synthesizer in Chrome) on your host computer, and you should hear the Middle C note play for 1 second!

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No MIDI Ports Found in Python:
    • Run lsmod | grep g_midi to check if the driver module is loaded in the kernel.
    • If it is not loaded, manually load it with sudo modprobe g_midi and check for errors.
  • Note on/off latency:
    • If you experience latency (delay) when triggering notes, ensure you are running a lightweight system loop. Using lower-level libraries like rtmidi directly or tuning CPU frequency governor to "performance" mode on your Raspberry Pi can reduce latency.
  • Linux Host Setup:
    • If connecting the Pi to a Linux host, you may need to map the virtual ports using aconnect or a patchbay tool like QjackCtl.

docs.title: How to Build an AI Smart Security Camera with Raspberry Pi and YOLOv8
How to Build an AI Smart Security Camera with Raspberry Pi and YOLOv8
docs.text:
Traditional security cameras rely on basic motion detection to trigger alerts. Unfortunately, this often leads to a storm of false notifications caused by wind blowing through trees, passing clouds, or insects flying in front of the lens.

By integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Object Detection, you can build a smart security camera that only alerts you when it detects specific objects of interest—such as a person, a car, or a dog.

In this guide, we will use YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once version 8), a state-of-the-art real-time object detection model developed by Ultralytics, on a Raspberry Pi. We will connect a camera, write a Python script to scan for people, and automatically send captured alert images directly to a Discord channel using webhooks.

docs.title: Performance Expectations
docs.text:
YOLOv8 is highly optimized, but running deep learning models is resource-intensive.

  • Model Selection: We will use YOLOv8n (Nano), the smallest version of the model. It has only 3.2 million parameters but offers excellent accuracy for common objects.
  • Frame Rates: Running natively on the CPU: * Raspberry Pi 5: Expect 10 to 15 FPS (sufficient for security surveillance). * Raspberry Pi 4: Expect 2 to 5 FPS (acceptable for slow-moving security sweeps, but can be accelerated using hardware like a Google Coral Edge TPU).

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi 4 (4GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5
  • Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 (or a standard USB webcam)
  • Power Supply
  • Internet Connection (to transmit the webhooks)

docs.title: Step 1: Connect and Test the Camera
docs.text:
Before writing the AI logic, ensure your camera interface is configured and working properly.

  1. Connect your Camera Module to the CSI port on the Pi (using the correct ribbon cable slot).
  2. Boot the Pi and run a quick test using the native libcamera suite: 
    libcamera-still -o test.jpg
  3. Verify that test.jpg is successfully saved in your directory. If you are using a USB webcam, you can test it using the utility fswebcam: 
    sudo apt install fswebcam -y
fswebcam test.jpg

docs.title: Step 2: Set Up the Python Virtual Environment
docs.text:
Installing AI packages globally can corrupt system-level dependencies. We will isolate PyTorch, OpenCV, and Ultralytics inside a virtual environment.

  1. Update the package repository: 
    sudo apt update
  2. Install Python virtual environment and OpenCV dependencies: 
    sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip libgl1-mesa-glx libglib2.0-0 -y
  3. Create the environment and activate it: 
    mkdir ~/smart-camera && cd ~/smart-camera
python3 -m venv camera-env
source camera-env/bin/activate
  4. Install the required libraries (this will download CPU-only PyTorch, OpenCV, and the Ultralytics suite): 
    pip install --upgrade pip
pip install ultralytics opencv-python requests

docs.title: Step 3: Write the Object Detection Script
docs.text:
We will write a script (security_camera.py) that captures frames from the camera, processes them through YOLOv8, detects if a "person" is present, and captures the frame.

To prevent spamming notifications, we will implement a cooldown timer (e.g., waiting 60 seconds before sending another alert).

Create the script: 

nano security_camera.py

Paste the following Python code:

import cv2
import time
import requests
from ultralytics import YOLO

# Configuration
DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL = "YOUR_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL_HERE"
COOLDOWN_SECONDS = 60
TARGET_CLASS_ID = 0  # Class ID for 'person' in the COCO dataset

# Initialize YOLOv8 Nano model
# The script will download 'yolov8n.pt' automatically on first run
model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")

# Initialize camera (0 is usually the default camera)
cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
if not cap.isOpened():
    print("Error: Could not open video source.")
    exit()

last_notification_time = 0

def send_discord_alert(frame):
    global last_notification_time
    current_time = time.time()

    # Check if we are still in the cooldown period
    if current_time - last_notification_time < COOLDOWN_SECONDS:
        print("Alert triggered, but skipped due to cooldown.")
        return

    print("Sending alert to Discord...")

    # Save the frame containing the detection
    image_path = "alert.jpg"
    cv2.imwrite(image_path, frame)

    # Send image to Discord via Webhook
    payload = {"content": "⚠️ Alert: Person detected by Smart Security Camera!"}
    with open(image_path, "rb") as f:
        files = {"file": (image_path, f, "image/jpeg")}
        try:
            response = requests.post(DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL, data=payload, files=files)
            if response.status_code == 200 or response.status_code == 204:
                print("Alert successfully sent.")
                last_notification_time = current_time
            else:
                print(f"Failed to send webhook: {response.status_code}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error sending webhook: {e}")

print("Smart Camera service started. Scanning...")

try:
    while True:
        ret, frame = cap.read()
        if not ret:
            print("Failed to grab frame.")
            break

        # Run inference (stream=True optimizes memory usage)
        results = model(frame, stream=True, verbose=False)

        person_detected = False
        for result in results:
            boxes = result.boxes
            for box in boxes:
                # Class 0 is 'person'
                class_id = int(box.cls[0])
                confidence = float(box.conf[0])

                # Filter out low-confidence detections (below 50%)
                if class_id == TARGET_CLASS_ID and confidence > 0.50:
                    person_detected = True
                    # Draw a bounding box for debugging/saved image
                    x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, box.xyxy[0])
                    cv2.rectangle(frame, (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (0, 0, 255), 2)
                    cv2.putText(frame, f"Person {confidence:.2f}", (x1, y1 - 10),
                                cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.5, (0, 0, 255), 2)

        if person_detected:
            send_discord_alert(frame)

        # Sleep slightly to prevent CPU maxing out on frame acquisition
        time.sleep(0.1)

finally:
    cap.release()
    cv2.destroyAllWindows()

docs.title: Step 4: Setting Up the Discord Webhook
docs.text:
To receive notifications on your phone or desktop:

  1. Open Discord and go to a server where you have administrator permissions.
  2. Open the settings of the channel where you want alerts to appear, click Integrations -> Webhooks -> Create Webhook.
  3. Copy the Webhook URL.
  4. Open security_camera.py and replace "YOUR_DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL_HERE" with the copied URL.

docs.title: Step 5: Run as a Background Daemon
docs.text:
To ensure the AI security camera runs automatically whenever the Raspberry Pi boots, set it up as a systemd service.

  1. Create a systemd unit file: 
    sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/smart-camera.service
  2. Add the configuration (replace pi with your username): 
    [Unit]
Description=YOLOv8 AI Smart Security Camera Service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=pi
WorkingDirectory=/home/pi/smart-camera
ExecStart=/home/pi/smart-camera/camera-env/bin/python security_camera.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
  3. Reload systemd, enable, and start the service: 
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable smart-camera.service
sudo systemctl start smart-camera.service
  4. Check the service status: 
    sudo systemctl status smart-camera.service

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Your DIY AI Security Camera is now scanning local frame feeds and dispatching alerts directly to your Discord channel. Because YOLOv8 analyzes the content of the image locally on the Pi, you will not receive alerts for background noise, maintaining high security and absolute data privacy.

docs.title: How to Create Docker Image of Raspberry Pi OS
How to Create Docker Image of Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text: This guide explains how to create a Docker image for Raspberry Pi OS on Ubuntu/Debian.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
First, download the Raspberry Pi OS OS image and unzip it:

wget https://downloads.raspberrypi.com/raspios_lite_armhf/images/raspios_lite_armhf-2024-11-19/2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img.xz
unzip 2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img.xz

docs.title: Inspect the OS Image
docs.text:
Use fdisk to inspect the image and identify partitions. We need Sector size and Start Sector of second image for mount. 

sudo fdisk --list 2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img
Disk 2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img: 2.38 GiB, 2550136832 bytes, 4980736 sectors
Units: sectors of 1 * 512 = 512 bytes
Sector size (logical/physical): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
I/O size (minimum/optimal): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
Disklabel type: dos
Disk identifier: 0x57b902f5

Device                                      Boot   Start     End Sectors  Size Id Type
2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img1         8192 1056767 1048576  512M  c W95 FAT32 (LBA)
2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img2      1056768 4980735 3923968  1.9G 83 Linux

docs.title: Mount and Create Docker Image
docs.text:
mkdir image
sudo mount -o loop,offset=$((512*1056768)) 2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.img image
cd image
sudo tar cf ../docker-image-2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.tar .

Import the archive as a Docker image: 

docker import docker-image-2024-11-19-raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite.tar raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite:2024-11-19

Check if the image is registered: 

docker image list

docs.title: Install qemu
docs.text:
If your host is x86_64, enable ARM emulation: 

sudo apt-get -y install qemu-user-static

docs.title: Running the Docker Image
docs.text:
Run the container: 

docker run -it raspios-bookworm-armhf-lite:2024-11-19 /bin/bash
uname -a
Linux f5f38b46dc55 6.1.0-31-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.1.128-1 (2025-02-07) armv7l GNU/Linux

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This guide outlines creating a Docker image from a Raspberry Pi OS image, importing it into Docker, and running it with QEMU emulation on non-ARM hosts.

docs.title: How to Monitor Raspberry Pi Performance with Prometheus and Grafana
How to Monitor Raspberry Pi Performance with Prometheus and Grafana
docs.text:
When running a Raspberry Pi as a 24/7 home server (hosting databases, media servers, or automation controllers), keeping an eye on system health is vital. If your Pi overheats, runs out of memory, or fills up its SD card, services will crash, and your files could face corruption.

Prometheus and Grafana are the industry-standard monitoring stack. Prometheus gathers and stores time-series metric data, while Grafana connects to Prometheus to turn those raw numbers into beautiful, interactive dashboards.

In this guide, we will deploy Prometheus, Grafana, and Node Exporter (the agent that extracts OS metrics) on a Raspberry Pi using Docker Compose. We will then import a pre-built dashboard to visualize CPU usage, RAM load, network traffic, and CPU temperatures in real-time.

docs.title: The Monitoring Stack Architecture
docs.text:
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|                      Your Raspberry Pi                    |
|                                                           |
|  [Node Exporter] --(Metrics on port 9100)--> [Prometheus] |
|        |                                           ^      |
|  (Reads OS Info & Temp)                            |      |
|                                            (Pulls Data)   |
|                                                    |      |
|  [Grafana Dashboard] <--(Reads Metrics)------------+      |
|        |                                                  |
|  (User Access on Port 3000)                               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
  1. Node Exporter: Runs directly on the Pi, collecting hardware and OS metrics (CPU load, memory, disk space, temperatures) and exposing them on a local web port.
  2. Prometheus: Connects to Node Exporter every few seconds, pulls (scrapes) the metrics, and saves them to an optimized database.
  3. Grafana: Connects to Prometheus to query the metrics and displays them on a web dashboard.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB+) or Raspberry Pi 5
  • Wired Ethernet Connection (recommended for stable dashboard updates)
  • Official Power Supply

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Docker Compose Configuration
docs.text:
We will deploy the entire stack using Docker Compose to ensure a modular setup.

  1. Create a project directory: 
    mkdir -p ~/pi-monitoring && cd ~/pi-monitoring
  2. Create the composition file: 
    nano docker-compose.yml
  3. Paste the following configuration:
version: '3.8'

services:
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    container_name: prometheus
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - ./prometheus_data:/prometheus
    command:
      - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml'
      - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus'
      - '--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d'
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"

  node-exporter:
    image: prom/node-exporter:latest
    container_name: node-exporter
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - /proc:/host/proc:ro
      - /sys:/host/sys:ro
      - /:/rootfs:ro
    command:
      - '--path.procfs=/host/proc'
      - '--path.sysfs=/host/sys'
      - '--collector.filesystem.ignored-mount-points=^/(sys|proc|dev|host|etc)($$|/)'
    ports:
      - "9100:9100"

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana-oss:latest
    container_name: grafana
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - ./grafana_data:/var/lib/grafana

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Prometheus Scraping
docs.text:
Before starting the containers, we must instruct Prometheus where to look for data.

  1. Create a configuration file: 
    nano prometheus.yml
  2. Paste the following scraping rules:
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s # How often to fetch metrics
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']

  - job_name: 'node-exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['node-exporter:9100'] # Target the node-exporter container
  1. Save the file and exit the editor.
  2. Start all services in background mode: 
    docker compose up -d

Ensure all three containers are running successfully: 

docker compose ps

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Grafana Web Dashboard
docs.text:
Once the services are running, we can build the frontend dashboard.

  1. Open your browser and navigate to: 
    http://<your-raspberry-pi-ip>:3000
  2. Log in using the default credentials: * Username: admin * Password: admin
  3. Set a new secure password when prompted.

docs.title: Adding Prometheus as a Data Source
docs.text:
1. On the Grafana homepage, click Connections -> Data sources.
  2. Click Add data source and select Prometheus.
  3. In the Connection settings, enter the URL of your Prometheus container: 
    http://prometheus:9090
  4. Scroll to the bottom and click Save & test. You should see a green checkmark saying "Data source is working".

docs.title: Step 4: Import the Node Exporter Dashboard
docs.text:
Creating a dashboard from scratch is time-consuming. We will import a popular, community-made dashboard ("Node Exporter Full") that instantly visualizes all typical server metrics.

  1. In the top-right corner of Grafana, click the + (plus icon) -> Import.
  2. Under Find and import dashboards, enter the official dashboard ID: 
    1860
  3. Click Load.
  4. On the next screen: * Select your folder (Default is fine). * At the bottom, under the Prometheus dropdown, select Prometheus (the data source we connected in Step 3).
  5. Click Import.

Your screen will instantly populate with live graphs showing CPU Core Usage, Memory Load, Disk IO, Network Bandwidth, and CPU Temperatures.

docs.title: Step 5: Customizing the Dashboard for CPU Temperature
docs.text:
Monitoring CPU thermal load is crucial on a Raspberry Pi because it will automatically throttle its clock speed (slowing down your apps) if it exceeds 80-85°C.

While the imported dashboard displays a small temperature reading, we can add a prominent Gauge panel for the temperature.

  1. On your dashboard, click Add (top right) -> Visualization.
  2. Select Prometheus as the query builder.
  3. In the Query box, enter the following Prometheus metric name: 
    node_hwmon_temp_celsius
  4. On the right-hand panel: * Change the panel type from Time series to Gauge. * Set the title to CPU Temperature. * Under Standard options, set the Unit to Celsius (°C). * Under Thresholds, set 70 to Orange and 80 to Red.
  5. Click Apply in the top right.
  6. Drag the new gauge to the top of your dashboard for quick verification. Click the floppy disk icon to save your dashboard layout.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Your Raspberry Pi is now continuously monitored by Prometheus. By utilizing Grafana, you can check system performance, observe thermal performance, and ensure your services run safely. You can also configure Grafana Alerting to send notifications (via Discord, Slack, or email) if the CPU temperature spikes or if disk space falls below 10%.

docs.title: How to Move Rootfs to External USB Storage
How to Move Rootfs to External USB Storage
Introduction
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi typically boots and runs its operating system from a microSD card. While convenient, microSD cards have limitations in terms of read/write speeds, longevity, and storage capacity. Moving the root filesystem (rootfs) to an external USB storage device, such as an SSD or USB flash drive, offers several significant advantages:

  • Improved Performance: SSD can provide read/write speeds many times faster than microSD cards
  • Enhanced Reliability: External storage often has better wear-leveling algorithms and longer lifespans
  • Increased Storage Capacity: External drives typically offer more space at a lower cost per gigabyte
  • Reduced Wear on SD Card: The SD card is only used for booting, minimizing write operations that can cause degradation

This guide explains how to move the root filesystem of a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm to an external USB storage device while keeping the boot partition on the SD card.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before beginning this procedure, ensure you have:

  • A Raspberry Pi with Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm installed
  • An external USB storage device (SSD, HDD, or USB flash drive)
  • A stable power supply for your Raspberry Pi and external drive
  • A backup of your important data
  • Access to terminal/SSH

docs.title: 1. Prepare Your External USB Storage
docs.text:
First, identify your external storage device and prepare it for use: 

sudo fdisk /dev/sdX
# Create a new partition (type Linux) and format it
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1

docs.title: 2. Mount the USB Storage
docs.text:
Create a mount point and mount the newly formatted partition: 

sudo mkdir /mnt/usb
sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/usb

docs.title: 3. Copy RootFS to USB
docs.text:
Use rsync to create an exact copy of your root filesystem on the external storage: 

sudo rsync -aAXv / --exclude={"/dev/*","/proc/*","/sys/*","/tmp/*","/run/*","/mnt/*","/media/*","/lost+found"} /mnt/usb

docs.title: 4. Modify Boot Configuration
docs.text:
Update the boot parameters to tell the Raspberry Pi to use the external storage for the root filesystem: 

sudo nano /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt
Change the root= parameter to point to your USB device, e.g., root=/dev/sdX1.

docs.title: 5. Reboot the Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Flush the filesystem buffers and restart your Raspberry Pi to apply the changes: 

sudo sync
sudo reboot

After rebooting, your Raspberry Pi should boot from the SD card but mount the root filesystem from the external USB storage.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
To verify the change was successful, check the current mount points:

df -h

You should see your external USB device mounted as / (root filesystem).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If your Raspberry Pi fails to boot:

  1. Remove the SD card and connect it to another computer
  2. Edit /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt to revert the root parameter to the original SD card partition
  3. Reinsert the SD card and boot the Raspberry Pi to try again

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Moving the root filesystem to external USB storage offers significant performance improvements and extends the life of your SD card. This configuration provides the reliability of USB storage for day-to-day operations while maintaining the simple bootloader on the SD card.

For optimal performance with SSDs, consider enabling TRIM support for your external drive and implementing regular maintenance practices such as periodic file system checks. This hybrid approach allows you to leverage the advantages of both storage mediums while minimizing their individual limitations.

Remember that different Raspberry Pi models have different USB capabilities—Raspberry Pi 4 and newer models with USB 3.0 ports will see the most substantial performance improvements when using high-speed external storage devices.

docs.title: How to Run a Discord Bot 24/7 on Raspberry Pi with Docker and Systemd
How to Run a Discord Bot 24/7 on Raspberry Pi with Docker and Systemd
docs.text:
Developing a custom Discord bot (using libraries like Python's discord.py or Node.js's discord.js) is a fun and rewarding project. However, hosting the bot on your personal development computer means it goes offline whenever your computer sleeps or shuts down.

While hosting in the cloud (AWS, Heroku, or VPS) is an option, it often incurs monthly fees. The Raspberry Pi is the perfect low-power, noiseless alternative for hosting bots 24/7 for free.

In this guide, we will cover two production-ready methods to run your Discord bot continuously in the background and configure auto-recovery in case of system crashes or network dropouts: * Method A: Systemd Service (Lightweight, native process execution) * Method B: Docker Compose (Containerized execution, version isolation)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Raspberry Pi (Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 3, 4, or 5).
  • Your bot application code transferred to the Pi (via Git or SSH).
  • A Discord Bot Token from the Discord Developer Portal.
  • Docker installed on the Pi (if using Method B).

docs.title: Step 1: Securing Your Token (Environment Variables)
docs.text:
Never hardcode your Discord Bot Token inside your source files. If you push your code to GitHub, your token will be exposed, compromised, and automatically revoked by Discord.

Instead, manage your credentials using an environment variable file (.env).

  1. In your bot project directory, create a .env file: 
    nano ~/my-discord-bot/.env
  2. Add your token and any configuration variables: 
    DISCORD_TOKEN=your_actual_bot_token_here
ENV=production
  3. Ensure your code loads these variables using libraries like python-dotenv (Python) or dotenv (Node.js). For example: * Python: 
    import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
TOKEN = os.getenv("DISCORD_TOKEN")
    * Node.js: 
    require('dotenv').config();
const token = process.env.DISCORD_TOKEN;

docs.title: Method A: Running Natively with Systemd
docs.text: Systemd is the built-in init system in Raspberry Pi OS. It allows you to run any script as a background daemon (service), automatically startup at boot, and restart if it crashes.

docs.title: 1. Create a Systemd Service File
docs.text:
Create a service configuration file: 

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/discord-bot.service

Add the following configuration (replace pi with your username, the working directory, and the path to your python/node binary):

[Unit]
Description=My Discord Bot Service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=pi
WorkingDirectory=/home/pi/my-discord-bot
EnvironmentFile=/home/pi/my-discord-bot/.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 bot.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Note: If your bot is written in Node.js, replace /usr/bin/python3 bot.py with /usr/bin/node index.js.

docs.title: 2. Manage the Service
docs.text:
Reload the systemd manager, enable the service to start at boot, and run it:

# Reload configurations
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

# Start the service
