While this is ideal for web hosting, media servers, and desktop use, it is problematic for robotics control, industrial automation, and audio synthesis. In these environments, missing a control loop deadline by a few milliseconds can cause physical damage, unstable motor feedback loops, or audio dropouts.

A Real-Time Linux Kernel (applying the PREEMPT_RT patch) changes the scheduler behavior. It makes almost all parts of the kernel preemptible, allowing high-priority user-space tasks to interrupt kernel threads immediately. This guarantees deterministic response times (low latency jitter) under heavy CPU loads.

This guide provides a comprehensive walkthrough for downloading, patching, configuring, and compiling a PREEMPT_RT kernel for the Raspberry Pi 5, followed by latency testing using the industry-standard cyclictest benchmark.

docs.title: 1. Real-Time vs. Standard Kernels
docs.text: gantt     title CPU Scheduling Comparison     dateFormat  X     axisFormat %s      section Standard Kernel     Low-priority task        :active, a1, 0, 10     System Interrupt (Kernel) :crit, a2, 10, 25     High-priority Task (Blocked) :a3, 25, 35      section PREEMPT_RT Kernel     Low-priority task        :active, b1, 0, 10     System Interrupt (Preempted) :crit, b2, 10, 12     High-priority Task (Immediate) :active, b3, 12, 22     System Interrupt (Resume) :crit, b4, 22, 35

docs.title: Technical Differences:
docs.text:
• Locking: Spinlocks are replaced with sleepable mutexes (rt_mutex). If a high-priority thread requests a resource held by a low-priority thread, the lock is preempted immediately using priority inheritance.
  • Interrupt Handling: In standard kernels, Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) run in a hard-interrupt context where scheduling is disabled. Under PREEMPT_RT, interrupts are forced into schedulable kernel threads (ksoftirqd), meaning they can be preempted.
  • Latency Jitter: While the average latency of standard kernels is low, they suffer from high max latency (jitter spikes). PREEMPT_RT caps the max latency to a predictable window (usually < 50 microseconds on Pi 5).

docs.title: 2. Setup Cross-Compilation Environment
docs.text: Compiling a Linux kernel on a Raspberry Pi 5 takes roughly 15 to 30 minutes. To save time and keep the Pi clean, it is highly recommended to cross-compile the kernel on a faster x86_64 host machine running Linux (Ubuntu/Debian).

docs.title: Step 1: Install Build Tools (On Host PC)
docs.text:
On your x86_64 Ubuntu/Debian build host, install the compiler toolchain and dependencies: 

sudo apt update
sudo apt install git bc bison flex libssl-dev make libc6-dev libncurses5-dev -y
sudo apt install crossbuild-essential-arm64 -y

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Workspace Directory
docs.text:
Create a dedicated workspace to host the kernel source tree and the patches: 

mkdir -p ~/rpi-kernel
cd ~/rpi-kernel

docs.title: 3. Downloading Kernel Source and the PREEMPT_RT Patch
docs.text: It is critical that the kernel source version matches the patch version exactly down to the minor release number.

docs.title: Step 1: Determine the Target Version
docs.text:
We will use the stable Linux 6.1.y branch (verify current stable RT branch versions on the kernel.org RT wiki). Clone the official Raspberry Pi kernel repository: 

# Clone the 6.1 branch specifically
git clone --depth=1 -b rpi-6.1.y https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux.git rpi-linux
cd rpi-linux

# Check the exact base version of the kernel
head -n 4 Makefile
This output displays the version structure: 
VERSION = 6
PATCHLEVEL = 1
SUBLEVEL = 77
EXTRAVERSION =
So, our base kernel version is 6.1.77. We must fetch the corresponding RT patch file.

docs.title: Step 2: Download the Matching RT Patch
docs.text:
Go back to the parent directory and download the patch corresponding to 6.1.77 from kernel.org: 

cd ~/rpi-kernel
curl -O https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/projects/rt/6.1/older/patch-6.1.77-rt24.patch.xz
Note: If a direct match does not exist, find the closest sublevel release.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply the Real-Time Patch
docs.text:
Navigate back into the kernel source tree and apply the compressed patch: 

cd rpi-linux
xzcat ../patch-6.1.77-rt24.patch.xz | patch -p1 --dry-run
If the dry run finishes without any errors, apply the patch for real: 
xzcat ../patch-6.1.77-rt24.patch.xz | patch -p1

docs.title: 4. Configuring the RT Kernel
docs.text: We need to generate a default configuration for the Raspberry Pi 5 processor (BCM2712) and enable the real-time scheduling flags.

docs.title: Step 1: Load Default Configuration
docs.text:
Run the default build configuration command for 64-bit Raspberry Pi boards: 

# Set cross-compiler variables
export ARCH=arm64
export CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu-

# Generate config file (.config)
make bcm2712_defconfig

docs.title: Step 2: Customize Kernel Options
docs.text:
Launch the menu configuration utility to modify the scheduler type: 

make menuconfig
Use the keyboard arrow keys and spacebar to navigate the menus and toggle the following options:

  1. Enable Fully Preemptible Kernel:

    • Go to General Setup --->
    • Go to Preemption Model --->
    • Select Fully Preemptible Kernel (Real-Time) (CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT=y).

  2. Disable Unneeded Virtualization/Tracing (Optional to reduce overhead):

    • Go to Kernel Hacking --->
    • Disable Kernel Debugging and Tracers (these add massive latency jitter).

  3. Check Timer Frequency:

    • Go to Kernel Features --->
    • Ensure Timer frequency is set to 1000 Hz (CONFIG_HZ_1000=y).

Save your settings and exit the menu configuration interface.

docs.title: 5. Compiling and Packaging the Kernel
docs.text: Now, build the kernel image, device trees, and module binaries.

docs.title: Step 1: Run the Compilation
docs.text:
Compile the kernel using all available CPU threads on your host PC (adjust -j parameter depending on your host core count, e.g., -j16): 

make -j$(nproc) Image modules dtbs
This process generates the uncompressed kernel image (arch/arm64/boot/Image) and device tree files (arch/arm64/boot/dts/broadcom/*.dtb).

docs.title: 6. Installing the Real-Time Kernel on Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text: To install the compiled files, mount your Raspberry Pi's SD card (or SSD) on your host PC, or transfer the compiled artifacts to the Pi over SSH. Here, we package the modules and transfer them to a running Pi 5 over SFTP.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Modules to a Temporary Directory (On Host PC)
docs.text:
cd ~/rpi-kernel/rpi-linux
mkdir -p ../rt-dist/boot
make INSTALL_MOD_PATH=../rt-dist modules_install

docs.title: Step 2: Copy Kernel Image and Device Trees
docs.text:
cp arch/arm64/boot/Image ../rt-dist/boot/kernel-rt.img
cp arch/arm64/boot/dts/broadcom/bcm2712-rpi-5-b.dtb ../rt-dist/boot/
cp -r arch/arm64/boot/dts/overlays ../rt-dist/boot/

docs.title: Step 3: Transfer to Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text:
Archive the built binaries, transfer them to the Pi, and unpack them: 

# Tar the directory
cd ~/rpi-kernel
tar -czf rt-kernel.tar.gz rt-dist

# Secure copy to Pi
scp rt-kernel.tar.gz pi@raspberrypi.local:/home/pi/

docs.title: Step 4: Install the Files (On the Raspberry Pi 5)
docs.text:
Log in to your Raspberry Pi 5 via SSH and install the files to their respective locations: 

# Logged into the Pi 5
cd /home/pi
tar -xzf rt-kernel.tar.gz

# Copy modules
sudo cp -r rt-dist/lib/modules/* /lib/modules/

# Backup original boot config and copy new images
sudo cp rt-dist/boot/kernel-rt.img /boot/firmware/
sudo cp rt-dist/boot/bcm2712-rpi-5-b.dtb /boot/firmware/
sudo cp -r rt-dist/boot/overlays/* /boot/firmware/overlays/

docs.title: Step 5: Configure Bootloader to use the RT Kernel
docs.text:
Open the bootloader config file: 

sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
Instruct the Pi bootloader to boot the new kernel-rt.img kernel: 
[all]
kernel=kernel-rt.img
Save the file and reboot the Raspberry Pi 5: 
sudo reboot

docs.title: 7. Latency Verification with cyclictest
docs.text:
Once the system boots, verify that the PREEMPT_RT kernel is running: 

uname -a
The output must show #1 SMP PREEMPT_RT in the version string: 
Linux raspberrypi 6.1.77-rt24-v8+ #1 SMP PREEMPT_RT Mon Jun 21 2026 aarch64 GNU/Linux

docs.title: Running the Latency Benchmark
docs.text:
Install the real-time test suite: 

sudo apt install rt-tests -y

Now, run cyclictest to measure latency jitter. We will run the test under heavy system load (simulate disk and CPU stress in a separate terminal using stress-ng or stress) to test worst-case performance: 

# In Terminal 1: Generate system load
sudo apt install stress -y
stress --cpu 4 --io 2 --vm 2 --vm-bytes 128M

# In Terminal 2: Run latency test for 100,000 cycles
sudo cyclictest --mlockall --smp --priority=99 --interval=200 --distance=0 --loops=100000

docs.title: Benchmark Interpretation:
docs.text:
# Output from a Standard Kernel:
T: 0 ( 1234) P:99 I:200 C:100000 Min:      4 Act:    8 Avg:   15 Max:   8450 (μs)

# Output from the PREEMPT_RT Kernel on Pi 5:
T: 0 ( 5678) P:99 I:200 C:100000 Min:      2 Act:    4 Avg:    6 Max:     28 (μs)
- Avg (Average Latency): Reduced from 15 microseconds to 6 microseconds. - Max (Maximum Jitter): The standard kernel hit a maximum latency spike of 8,450 μs (8.4 ms), which would ruin precise motor loops. The PREEMPT_RT kernel capped the maximum spike to 28 μs (0.028 ms), keeping the control loop perfectly deterministic.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: By deploying a custom PREEMPT_RT kernel, your Raspberry Pi 5 is transformed into an industrial-grade controller capable of executing tight control loops (e.g., 1000 Hz CAN Bus communications, EtherCAT drives, or custom PWM motor controllers) with microsecond precision. Keep kernel-debugging flags disabled to ensure peak deterministic execution.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Keyboard customization is an effective way to improve productivity and ergonomics when using your Raspberry Pi. One of the most popular customizations among programmers, system administrators, and power users is remapping the Caps Lock key to function as an additional Control key.

This modification offers several notable advantages:

  • Ergonomic Benefit: The Control key is heavily used in command-line interfaces and text editors, but its traditional position in the bottom corner of the keyboard can cause hand strain. The Caps Lock key is more centrally located and easier to reach.
  • Productivity Improvement: Most users rarely need Caps Lock, while Control is used frequently for keyboard shortcuts in terminals, code editors, and many applications.
  • Historical Context: This modification follows a tradition from Unix/Linux power users and programmers who value efficient keyboard usage.

This guide explains how to remap the Caps Lock key to function as a Control key on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm using the labwc window manager configuration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before proceeding, ensure you have:

  • Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm installed
  • Basic familiarity with text editors (nano, vim, etc.)
  • Administrative access to your Raspberry Pi

docs.title: 1. Locate or Create the Environment Configuration File
docs.text:
The labwc window manager (used in Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm) reads environment settings from a specific configuration file:

  • After initially configuring your keyboard settings using raspi-config, the file ~/.config/labwc/environment should be created with your keyboard configurations.
  • If this file doesn't exist, you'll need to create it manually:
# Create the directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p ~/.config/labwc

# Create or edit the environment file
nano ~/.config/labwc/environment

docs.title: 2. Modify the Configuration to Remap Caps Lock
docs.text:
The X Keyboard Extension (XKB) provides options for customizing keyboard behavior. You can choose between two common remapping approaches:

  • Open ~/.config/labwc/environment in a text editor.
  • Add one of the following configuration lines:

Option 1: Convert Caps Lock to Control (most common) 

XKB_DEFAULT_OPTIONS=ctrl:nocaps
This makes Caps Lock function as a Control key, effectively giving you an additional, more ergonomically positioned Control key.

Option 2: Swap Caps Lock and Control 

XKB_DEFAULT_OPTIONS=ctrl:swapcaps
This completely exchanges the functions of the Caps Lock and left Control keys.

docs.title: 3. Apply the Changes
docs.text:
After making changes to the configuration file, you need to apply them:

  • Either log out and log back in for changes to take effect, or
  • Execute the following command to reconfigure labwc without logging out:
labwc --reconfig

You can test the new key mapping by opening a terminal and using keyboard shortcuts that require the Control key, such as Ctrl+C to interrupt a command or Ctrl+L to clear the screen.

docs.title: Additional Customization Options
docs.text:
The XKB system supports many other keyboard customizations beyond remapping Caps Lock. You can combine multiple options by separating them with commas:

XKB_DEFAULT_OPTIONS=ctrl:nocaps,altwin:swap_alt_win

Some other useful options include:

  • altwin:swap_alt_win: Swap Alt and Windows/Super keys
  • compose:ralt: Use right Alt as Compose key for special characters
  • terminate:ctrl_alt_bksp: Enable Ctrl+Alt+Backspace to restart the X server

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Remapping the Caps Lock key to Control is a small change that can significantly improve your typing efficiency and comfort when working on your Raspberry Pi. This modification is particularly valuable for users who frequently work with terminal commands, programming editors, or any software that makes heavy use of Control key combinations.

For users who spend considerable time on their Raspberry Pi for development or system administration tasks, this customization can reduce hand strain and improve productivity. Combined with other ergonomic practices and customizations, keyboard remapping helps create a more comfortable and efficient computing environment tailored to your specific needs.

Remember that keyboard preferences are highly personal—experiment with different configurations to find what works best for your workflow.

docs.title: Running a Lightweight Kubernetes Cluster (k3s) on Raspberry Pi
Running a Lightweight Kubernetes Cluster (k3s) on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Running a Kubernetes cluster on Raspberry Pi is an excellent way to learn production-grade container orchestration, set up a home lab, or deploy highly available microservices. While standard Kubernetes (kubeadm) is too heavy for the Pi's limited RAM, k3s by Rancher is a highly optimized, fully compliant lightweight alternative designed specifically for edge and IoT environments.

This guide walks you through setting up a k3s cluster from scratch on Raspberry Pi OS.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites and Planning
docs.text: For a functional Kubernetes cluster, we recommend: - At least two Raspberry Pi devices (Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with 4GB/8GB RAM are highly recommended. A 1GB/2GB Pi is too small for running multiple workloads). - Wired Ethernet connection (Wi-Fi is prone to packet loss, which causes nodes to flap to offline states). - Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) (essential for running 64-bit container architectures).

docs.title: 2. Preparing the OS (Cgroups Configuration)
docs.text:
Kubernetes relies on Linux Control Groups (cgroups) to limit CPU and memory allocation for pods. By default, memory cgroups are disabled in Raspberry Pi OS and must be explicitly enabled.

Run this step on all nodes (Server and Agents):

docs.title: 1. Edit the Boot Command Line
docs.text:
Open /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt (or /boot/cmdline.txt on older OS versions) using sudo:

sudo nano /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt

docs.title: 2. Append Parameters
docs.text:
Add the following options to the end of the existing single line (do not insert newlines):

cgroup_enable=cpuset cgroup_memory=1 cgroup_enable=memory

docs.title: 3. Reboot the system
docs.text: sudo reboot

docs.title: 4. Verify Cgroup Support
docs.text:
After rebooting, check that the memory cgroup is enabled: 

cat /proc/cgroups | grep memory

docs.title: 3. Installing the k3s Server (Master Node)
docs.text:
On your designated Master Node, run the official k3s installation script:

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -

This script: - Downloads the k3s binary. - Configures a systemd service (k3s). - Installs kubectl, ctr, and other standard container tools. - Starts the Kubernetes API server.

docs.title: Verify Server Operation
docs.text:
Once the installation finishes, run:

sudo kubectl get nodes
You should see your master node in a Ready state: 
NAME           STATUS   ROLES                  AGE   VERSION
raspberrypi1   Ready    control-plane,master   35s   v1.28.2+k3s1

docs.title: Retrieve the Connection Token
docs.text:
To connect worker nodes to this master, you need the unique node token generated by the server. Retrieve it by running:

sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token
(Copy the resulting string; you will need it for the next step).

docs.title: 4. Connecting Worker Nodes (Agent Nodes)
docs.text:
On your Worker Nodes (Agent nodes), run the installation script, specifying your Master Node's IP address and the Token you copied:

# Define environment variables
export K3S_URL="https://192.168.1.100:6443"
export K3S_TOKEN="K10fef8b8c1..." # Paste your actual token here

# Run installer in agent mode
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -

The script automatically registers the agent to the master server and starts the k3s-agent service.

docs.title: Verify Cluster Status
docs.text:
Go back to your Master Node and run:

sudo kubectl get nodes
You should now see all connected nodes: 
NAME           STATUS   ROLES                  AGE    VERSION
raspberrypi1   Ready    control-plane,master   10m    v1.28.2+k3s1
raspberrypi2   Ready    <none>                 2m     v1.28.2+k3s1

docs.title: 5. Deploying a Workload
docs.text: Let's verify the cluster's orchestration capabilities by deploying a simple web server workload.

docs.title: 1. Create a Deployment file (web-deploy.yaml)
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rpi-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
      nodePort: 30080

docs.title: 2. Apply the configuration
docs.text:
On the master node, deploy the YAML file:

sudo kubectl apply -f web-deploy.yaml

docs.title: 3. Verify Pod Status
docs.text:
sudo kubectl get pods -o wide
You will see two web server pods running, likely distributed across different physical Raspberry Pi devices: 
NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTART   IP           NODE
rpi-web-84f98d45d6-abc12   1/1     Running   0         10.42.1.3    raspberrypi2
rpi-web-84f98d45d6-xyz34   1/1     Running   0         10.42.0.5    raspberrypi1

Access the web server from any browser on your local network by navigating to http://<ANY_PI_IP>:30080.

docs.title: 6. Resource Management & Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Configure Swap Space: Kubernetes expects Swap to be disabled by default. While k3s can run with Swap enabled, it can cause unstable scheduling. Set memory limits on your pods to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killing.
  2. Watch Storage wear: Running etcd/k3s logs writes constantly to disk. Use High-End SD cards (A1 or A2 rated) or boot from SSDs to prevent storage failure.
  3. Set Up a Local Registry: Pulling heavy Docker images over the internet on multiple Pi nodes can saturate local network bandwidth. Consider setting up a local Docker registry.

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text:
• Optimizing Swap with ZRAM — Prevent memory exhaustion crashes under heavy workloads.
  • Static IP Configuration — Set persistent IPs for your Kubernetes API server.

docs.title: Secure Home Server: Expose Nextcloud/Jellyfin without Port Forwarding via Cloudflare Tunnel
Secure Home Server: Expose Nextcloud/Jellyfin without Port Forwarding via Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.text:
Hosting personal servers like Nextcloud (for private files) or Jellyfin (for home media streaming) on a Raspberry Pi is a fantastic way to regain control of your personal data. However, exposing these services to the internet traditionally required configuring dynamic DNS, punching holes in your router's firewall via port forwarding (opening ports 80/443), and risking direct attacks on your home network IP address.

This guide provides a secure, modern alternative: Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared). By establishing an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare's nearest edge server, you can securely route external traffic to your Raspberry Pi without exposing your residential IP address or opening any incoming router ports.

docs.title: 1. Cloudflare Tunnel Architecture
docs.text:
Unlike typical reverse proxies that listen for incoming connections, cloudflared initiates secure, encrypted outbound connections (over ports 7844/443) to Cloudflare’s global network.

graph LR A[Client Browser] -->|HTTPS| B(Cloudflare Edge) B -->|Encrypted Cloudflare Tunnel| C[cloudflared Daemon on Pi] C -->|Local Routing| D[Local Services: Nextcloud, Jellyfin]

docs.title: Advantages of Cloudflare Tunnels:
docs.text:
• No Port Forwarding: Protects your local network from open-port scanners.
  • DDoS Protection: Cloudflare automatically mitigates volumetric attacks at the edge before they reach your Raspberry Pi.
  • Hidden Residential IP: Attackers see Cloudflare IPs, not your home router's public address.
  • SSL/TLS by Default: SSL certificates are managed automatically by Cloudflare at the edge.

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites & Cloudflare Setup
docs.text: Before starting, ensure you have: 1. A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 running Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit). 2. A custom domain name (e.g., yourdomain.com). 3. A free Cloudflare Account, with your custom domain's nameservers pointed to Cloudflare (allowing Cloudflare to manage your DNS records).

docs.title: 3. Installing cloudflared on Raspberry Pi
docs.text: The cloudflared agent needs to be installed on your Raspberry Pi to establish the tunnel.

docs.title: Step 1: Add the Cloudflare Package Repository
docs.text:
Download and install the official Cloudflare GPG key, then add the repository source: 

# Create directory for keyrings
sudo mkdir -p --mode=0755 /usr/share/keyrings

# Download the key
curl -fsSL https://pkg.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-main.gpg | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/cloudflare-main.gpg > /dev/null

# Add repository to sources list
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/cloudflare-main.gpg] https://pkg.cloudflare.com/cloudflared bullseye main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/cloudflared.list

# Update package lists and install cloudflared
sudo apt update
sudo apt install cloudflared -y

Verify that the binary is installed and running correctly: 

cloudflared --version

docs.title: 4. Authenticating and Creating the Tunnel
docs.text: Now, establish a connection between the local cloudflared binary and your Cloudflare DNS account.

docs.title: Step 1: Authenticate the Daemon
docs.text:
Execute the login command: 

cloudflared tunnel login
This command output will display a unique URL: 
Please open the following URL and log in with your Cloudflare account:
https://dash.cloudflare.com/argotunnel?callback=https%3A%2F%2Fpkg.cloudflare.com%2F...
Copy and paste this URL into your web browser. Log in, select your domain (yourdomain.com), and click Authorize. This downloads a certificate key file (cert.pem) to /home/pi/.cloudflare/cert.pem (or your user's home directory).

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Named Tunnel
docs.text:
Create a new tunnel naming it after your server (e.g., pi-homelab): 

cloudflared tunnel create pi-homelab
This outputs a unique UUID for your tunnel and creates a credentials JSON file: 
Created tunnel pi-homelab with id 12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab
Credentials file written to /home/pi/.cloudflare/12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab.json
Keep this UUID safe, as we will use it in the configuration files next.

docs.title: 5. Local Tunnel Configuration & Routing
docs.text: Now configure cloudflared to route incoming traffic for specific subdomains to your local services (Nextcloud, Jellyfin, etc.).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Configuration File
docs.text:
Create the configuration directory and file: 

sudo mkdir -p /etc/cloudflared
sudo nano /etc/cloudflared/config.yml

Add the following YAML configuration, replacing the tunnel UUID, file path, and domain with your actual values: 

# /etc/cloudflared/config.yml
tunnel: 12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab
credentials-file: /etc/cloudflared/12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab.json

ingress:
  # Route traffic for nextcloud.yourdomain.com to local Nextcloud container
  - hostname: nextcloud.yourdomain.com
    service: http://localhost:8080

  # Route traffic for jellyfin.yourdomain.com to local Jellyfin server
  - hostname: jellyfin.yourdomain.com
    service: http://localhost:8096

  # Default rule: A 404 handler for any unmapped requests
  - service: http_status:404

Copy the credentials JSON file to /etc/cloudflared/ for centralized management: 

sudo cp /home/pi/.cloudflare/12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab.json /etc/cloudflared/

docs.title: Step 2: Associate DNS Records in Cloudflare
docs.text:
Bind your subdomains to the tunnel UUID. This creates CNAME records pointing to your tunnel domain: 

cloudflared tunnel route dns pi-homelab nextcloud.yourdomain.com
cloudflared tunnel route dns pi-homelab jellyfin.yourdomain.com

docs.title: Step 3: Test the Tunnel
docs.text:
Launch the tunnel in debug mode to ensure there are no formatting or connection errors: 

cloudflared --config /etc/cloudflared/config.yml tunnel run
Look for logs showing successful connection connections to Cloudflare's edge data centers: 
INF Connection 12345678-abcd-1234-abcd-1234567890ab established
INF Route nextcloud.yourdomain.com to http://localhost:8080
Open a browser and navigate to https://nextcloud.yourdomain.com. You should see your Nextcloud login screen over a secure SSL/TLS connection! Press Ctrl+C to stop the debug test.

docs.title: 6. Configuring cloudflared as a systemd Service
docs.text: For a robust home lab setup, the tunnel must run persistently in the background and start automatically on boot.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the Service
docs.text:
cloudflared has a built-in helper command to install itself as a systemd service: 

sudo cloudflared --config /etc/cloudflared/config.yml service install
This automatically configures a service file /etc/systemd/system/cloudflared.service.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable and Start the Daemon
docs.text:
Reload systemd, enable the service to launch on boot, and start it now: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable cloudflared
sudo systemctl start cloudflared

docs.title: Step 3: Monitor Service Health
docs.text:
Check the status of the tunnel: 

sudo systemctl status cloudflared
You can also follow the live systemd journal logs to debug connections: 
sudo journalctl -u cloudflared -f

docs.title: 7. Zero Trust Security: Access Control Policies
docs.text:
Exposing services like Nextcloud or Jellyfin to the public web means hackers can attempt brute-force login attacks on your application pages. To prevent this, you can put Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust) in front of your subdomains to enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) before anyone can even reach the login screen of your Raspberry Pi.

graph TD A[Unauthenticated Request] --> B(Cloudflare Access) B -->|Pass Google/GitHub Auth| C(Nextcloud Login Page) B -->|Fail Auth| D[Access Denied 403]

docs.title: Implementing Cloudflare Access Rules:
docs.text:
1. Log in to the Cloudflare Dashboard and click on Zero Trust in the left sidebar.
  2. Navigate to Access > Applications and click Add an Application.
  3. Select Self-hosted.
  4. Configure the Application:
    • Application Name: Nextcloud Secure Auth
    • Domain: nextcloud.yourdomain.com
  5. Configure the Identity Providers:
    • Add Google or GitHub as authentication providers under Zero Trust Settings.
  6. Configure the Policy:
    • Policy Name: Allow Owner Only
    • Action: Allow
    • Rules: Select Emails or Emails Ending In and type your email address (e.g., owner@gmail.com).
  7. Save the Application.

Now, navigating to https://nextcloud.yourdomain.com will prompt a Cloudflare Access screen asking you to sign in with your GitHub or Google account. Only after validation will Cloudflare pass your connection through to the Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: You now have a secure home lab environment exposed to the internet with zero open incoming ports. External visitors pass through Cloudflare's edge firewall, mitigating port-scans and DDoS attacks, while Cloudflare Zero Trust secures your administrative consoles with modern OAuth single sign-on.

docs.title: Secure Infrastructure: Secure Remote Connections with WireGuard and Pi-hole on Raspberry Pi
Secure Infrastructure: Secure Remote Connections with WireGuard and Pi-hole on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
When browsing the web on public Wi-Fi networks (such as in hotels or cafes), your internet traffic is vulnerable to eavesdropping and local man-in-the-middle attacks. Additionally, browsing from mobile devices consumes significant cellular data loading ads and tracking scripts.

By setting up a WireGuard VPN (Virtual Private Network) server on your Raspberry Pi and routing its DNS requests through a local Pi-hole, you construct a powerful secure remote gateway: - Encrypted Tunneling: All your network traffic is encrypted and tunneled securely to your home Raspberry Pi before entering the internet. - On-The-Go Ad Blocking: Your mobile device uses the home Pi-hole as its secure DNS resolver, blocking ads and tracking domains globally across cellular and external networks. - Secure LAN Access: Access other local home lab servers (such as NAS shares or smart home dashboards) from anywhere without exposing them directly to the web.

This guide provides a comprehensive tutorial for installing WireGuard via PiVPN, configuring DNS forwarding to a local Pi-hole instance, setting up mobile clients, and routing split-tunnel traffic for optimal performance.

docs.title: 1. Network Architecture
docs.text:
When activated on a client, all traffic or DNS requests are securely sent to the Raspberry Pi over an encrypted UDP port.

graph TD subgraph Client Device (Mobile/Laptop) A[Client Browser/App] -->|Encrypted VPN Tunnel| B[WireGuard Client Interface] end subgraph Home Network (Raspberry Pi) B -->|UDP Port 51820| C[WireGuard Server Interface wg0] C -->|DNS Queries| D[Pi-hole Resolver] D -->|Ad Blocked Queries| C C -->|Web Traffic| E[WAN / Internet Gateway] end

Using WireGuard instead of older protocols (like OpenVPN) provides major advantages for mobile devices: - Low Power Consumption: WireGuard is implemented directly in the Linux kernel space and sleeps when not transmitting data, conserving smartphone battery. - Roaming Support: If you switch from Wi-Fi to a 4G/5G cellular network, WireGuard instantly re-establishes the tunnel connection without dropping active sessions.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up Pi-hole
docs.text:
If you do not have Pi-hole installed on your Raspberry Pi, install it using the official automated installer script: 

curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash
Follow the interactive prompt instructions: - Assign a static IP address to your Raspberry Pi. - Select an upstream DNS provider (e.g., Cloudflare or Google). - Note down the automatically generated administrator web interface password.

docs.title: 3. Installing WireGuard via PiVPN
docs.text: The easiest and most secure way to install and configure WireGuard on Raspberry Pi OS is using the PiVPN tool wrapper.

docs.title: Step 1: Run the PiVPN Installer
docs.text:
Execute the installation script: 

curl -L https://install.pivpn.io | bash

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Installer Steps
docs.text:
Follow the guided steps on your terminal: 1. Detect Static IP: The installer checks that your Pi has a static IP address. Confirm it. 2. Choose User: Select the default system user (usually pi) to store VPN configuration profiles. 3. Select VPN Protocol: Select WireGuard (highly recommended over OpenVPN). 4. Default Port: Accept the default WireGuard port: 51820 (UDP). 5. DNS Provider: The installer will detect your running Pi-hole server and ask: 

Do you want to use your local Pi-hole as the DNS server for VPN clients?
Select Yes. 6. Public IP or DNS: Specify your home router's public WAN IP address. If your home IP changes dynamically, enter your Dynamic DNS domain name (e.g., yourhost.ddns.net).

After completion, restart the Raspberry Pi: 

sudo reboot

docs.title: 4. Configuring Port Forwarding on Your Router
docs.text:
For external clients to connect to the WireGuard server on the Raspberry Pi, your home router must forward incoming UDP traffic on port 51820 to the static IP address of the Pi.

  1. Log in to your home router's administrative dashboard (typically 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1).
  2. Navigate to the Port Forwarding / Virtual Server settings page.
  3. Add a new port forwarding rule:
    • Internal IP: The static IP of your Raspberry Pi (e.g., 192.168.1.100).
    • External Port: 51820
    • Internal Port: 51820
    • Protocol: UDP (Do not use TCP; WireGuard runs exclusively over UDP).
  4. Save and apply the configuration changes.

docs.title: 5. Adding and Configuring Client Profiles
docs.text: Once the server is running, generate unique configuration profiles for each client device (e.g. your smartphone and laptop).

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Client Profile
docs.text:
Run the PiVPN client command on your Raspberry Pi: 

pivpn add
Enter a distinct name for the client when prompted (e.g., iphone): 
Enter a Name for the Client: iphone
::: Client 'iphone' added, config file created at: /home/pi/configs/iphone.conf

docs.title: Step 2: Connect a Mobile Device (QR Code)
docs.text:
To configure a smartphone, you can render the configuration file as a QR code directly in the terminal, then scan it with the mobile app: 

pivpn -qr iphone
1. Install the official WireGuard application from the Apple App Store or Google Play Store. 2. Open the app on your phone and tap the + (Add) button. 3. Select Create from QR code and scan the QR code displayed on your Pi's terminal screen. 4. Name the tunnel "Home VPN" and toggle it ON.

docs.title: 6. Tuning Pi-hole for VPN Client Queries
docs.text:
By default, Pi-hole only answers DNS queries originating from the same local subnet (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24). Because WireGuard clients connect from a virtual VPN subnet (typically 10.6.0.0/24), you must tell Pi-hole to permit queries from other interfaces.

  1. Open your web browser and log in to the Pi-hole Admin Console (http://<your-pi-ip>/admin).
  2. Navigate to Settings > DNS.
  3. Scroll down to the Interface settings section.
  4. Change the selection from Show only local networks to Permit all origins (or Respond only on interface wg0 depending on your version).
  5. Scroll to the bottom and click Save.

docs.title: 7. Optimizing Tunnel Routing: Full Tunnel vs. Split Tunnel
docs.text:
You can configure what traffic goes through the VPN by editing the AllowedIPs parameter in the client configuration profile.

# Full Tunnel Configuration:
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0
# All traffic (web browsing, apps, and DNS) is encrypted and routed through the Pi.

# Split Tunnel Configuration:
AllowedIPs = 192.168.1.0/24, 10.6.0.0/24
# Only local home network traffic is routed through the Pi. General web browsing 
# goes directly to the internet via the client's current network, saving home bandwidth.

To modify this, edit the client configuration file on the client device (e.g., inside the WireGuard mobile app settings under Allowed IPs).

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: By combining WireGuard and Pi-hole, you have configured a secure, high-performance remote access gateway. External devices can browse safely on public Wi-Fi networks with automatic ad blocking and secure access to your home lab.

docs.title: Secure Remote Access to Raspberry Pi using Tailscale (No Port Forwarding)
Secure Remote Access to Raspberry Pi using Tailscale (No Port Forwarding)
docs.text: Access your Raspberry Pi from anywhere in the world without exposing ports on your home router! This step-by-step guide explains how to install and configure Tailscale to create a secure, encrypted mesh VPN network for easy remote access.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Traditionally, accessing your Raspberry Pi from outside your home network required configuring Dynamic DNS (DDNS) and setting up Port Forwarding on your home router. This process is not only complicated but also exposes your home network to malicious scans and attacks.

Tailscale solves this problem by using the modern WireGuard protocol to establish secure, peer-to-peer connections (a "mesh VPN"). It traverses firewalls and NATs automatically, meaning you do not need to open any ports on your router.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Tailscale on the Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Tailscale provides an automated installation script that detects your Raspberry Pi OS version and configures the repository.

  1. Connect to your Raspberry Pi locally (via terminal or local SSH).
  2. Run the official Tailscale installation script: 
    curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
  3. Once the installation completes, the Tailscale daemon will start automatically.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect the Raspberry Pi to Your Tailnet
docs.text:
Now, authenticate your Raspberry Pi to associate it with your Tailscale account (your "Tailnet").

  1. Run the login command: 
    sudo tailscale up
  2. The terminal will print a unique authentication URL: 
    To authenticate, visit:
https://login.tailscale.com/a/a1b2c3d4e5f6
  3. Copy this URL, paste it into a web browser on your PC or phone, and sign in (using Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or email).
  4. Click Authorize to connect the Raspberry Pi to your network.
  5. Back in the terminal, you should see: 
    Success.

To find your Raspberry Pi's new private Tailscale IP address, run: 

tailscale ip -4
This IP address (usually starting with 100.x.y.z) is static and belongs only to your private network.

docs.title: Step 3: Remote Connect from Your Client Devices
docs.text:
To access your Raspberry Pi remotely, you must install Tailscale on the device you want to connect from (such as your laptop, desktop, or smartphone).

  1. Download and install Tailscale on your client device from tailscale.com/download.
  2. Launch the Tailscale app and sign in with the same account you used for the Raspberry Pi.
  3. Once connected, your client device and Raspberry Pi are part of the same secure virtual network.

docs.title: Test SSH Access
docs.text:
From your laptop (connected to any network, e.g., cellular data or public Wi-Fi), run: 

ssh username@your-pi-tailscale-ip

docs.title: Test VNC Desktop Access
docs.text: If you use VNC for graphical desktop access, open your VNC Viewer client and enter your Raspberry Pi's Tailscale IP address (e.g., 100.80.90.100) to log in.

docs.title: Advanced: Configure the Pi as an Exit Node
docs.text: You can configure your Raspberry Pi to act as an Exit Node. This routes all of your client device's internet traffic through your home network—useful for securing your connection when using untrusted public Wi-Fi.

docs.title: 1. Enable IP Forwarding on the Pi:
docs.text:
Edit the sysctl file: 

sudo nano /etc/sysctl.conf
Uncomment the following lines to allow IP forwarding: 
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
Save the file and apply the changes: 
sudo sysctl -p

docs.title: 2. Advertise the Exit Node:
docs.text:
Restart Tailscale on the Pi with the exit-node flag: 

sudo tailscale up --advertise-exit-node

docs.title: 3. Approve the Exit Node:
docs.text:
1. Open the Tailscale Admin Console.
  2. Locate your Raspberry Pi in the machine list.
  3. Click the three dots menu (...) next to it, select Edit route settings, and toggle on Use as exit node.

Now, from the Tailscale app on your phone or laptop, you can select your Raspberry Pi as the "Exit Node" to secure your web browsing.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Tailscale cannot connect:
    • Run sudo systemctl status tailscaled to verify that the daemon is running.
    • If it is stopped, run sudo systemctl enable --now tailscaled.
  • Latency is high:
    • By default, Tailscale attempts to make a direct peer-to-peer connection. If it fails due to strict NAT firewalls, it relays traffic through encrypted DERP servers, which increases latency. You can check connection status by running tailscale status.

docs.title: Secure Self-Hosting: Docker Compose and Nginx Proxy Manager on Raspberry Pi
Secure Self-Hosting: Docker Compose and Nginx Proxy Manager on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Running self-hosted services (like a private cloud, password manager, or ad-blocker) on a single Raspberry Pi is highly efficient. However, as you add more services, you run into port conflicts (e.g. multiple services wanting port 80/443) and the complexity of managing SSL certificates for secure HTTPS access.

This guide shows you how to resolve port conflicts and configure automatic HTTPS routing using Docker Compose and Nginx Proxy Manager.

docs.title: 1. Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Rather than exposing multiple custom ports (like http://192.168.1.100:8080 or http://192.168.1.100:3000) to your local network, a Reverse Proxy intercepts all traffic on standard HTTP/HTTPS ports (80/443) and routes requests to the correct container based on the incoming domain name.

                  Local Network Client (Browser)
                                │
                        (e.g., vault.local)
                                │
                                ▼
                  Nginx Proxy Manager (Port 80/443)
            ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐
            │ (Proxy Pass)                          │ (Proxy Pass)
            ▼                                       ▼
    Vaultwarden (Port 8080)                  Pi-hole Admin (Port 8081)

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure you have Docker and Docker Compose installed on your Raspberry Pi:

# Install Docker
curl -sSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Install Docker Compose dependencies
sudo apt install -y python3-pip libffi-dev

Note: Log out and log back in to apply the group membership.

docs.title: 3. The Unified Docker Compose Configuration
docs.text:
Create a dedicated directory for your server setup and create a docker-compose.yml file:

mkdir -p ~/selfhost && cd ~/selfhost
nano docker-compose.yml

Paste the following configurations. This starts Nginx Proxy Manager (handling SSL and routing), Vaultwarden (lightweight Bitwarden password manager server), and Pi-hole (DNS ad-blocker):

version: '3.8'

networks:
  proxy-tier:
    name: proxy-tier

services:
  # Nginx Proxy Manager (Reverse Proxy)
  npm:
    image: 'jc21/nginx-proxy-manager:latest'
    container_name: npm
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '80:80'   # Public HTTP Port
      - '443:443' # Public HTTPS Port
      - '81:81'   # Admin Web Port
    volumes:
      - ./npm/data:/data
      - ./npm/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt
    networks:
      - proxy-tier

  # Vaultwarden (Password Manager)
  vaultwarden:
    image: 'vaultwarden/server:latest'
    container_name: vaultwarden
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - WEBSOCKET_ENABLED=true
    volumes:
      - ./vaultwarden:/data
    networks:
      - proxy-tier
    # Note: No ports are exposed to the host! Only the proxy can access it.

  # Pi-hole (Ad-blocker & Local DNS Server)
  pihole:
    image: 'pihole/pihole:latest'
    container_name: pihole
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '53:53/tcp' # DNS Ports must be host-exposed
      - '53:53/udp'
    environment:
      - TZ=UTC
      - WEBPASSWORD=ChooseSecureAdminPassword
    volumes:
      - ./pihole/etc-pihole:/etc/pihole
      - ./pihole/etc-dnsmasq.d:/etc/dnsmasq.d
    networks:
      - proxy-tier

docs.title: Launching the Stack
docs.text:
Start all services in detached background mode:

docker compose up -d

docs.title: 1. Log in to the Admin Panel
docs.text: Open your browser and navigate to http://<RASPBERRY_PI_IP>:81. - Default Email: admin@example.com - Default Password: changeme (You will be prompted to change these details immediately upon login).

docs.title: 2. Add a Proxy Host
docs.text:
Let's route vault.local to the Vaultwarden container: 1. Click Hosts $\rightarrow$ Proxy Hosts $\rightarrow$ Add Proxy Host. 2. Domain Names: Enter vault.local (or a domain name you own). 3. Scheme: Select http. 4. Forward Hostname / IP: Enter the container name: vaultwarden. (Because they share the same Docker network, Docker's internal DNS resolves this name). 5. Forward Port: Enter 80 (Vaultwarden's internal listening port). 6. Enable Block Common Exploits and Websockets Support.

    Domain Names: vault.local
    Scheme: http
    Forward Hostname: vaultwarden
    Forward Port: 80

docs.title: 3. Configure SSL (HTTPS)
docs.text:
Under the SSL tab: 1. Select Request a new SSL Certificate from the SSL Certificate dropdown. 2. Check Force SSL and HTTP/2 Support. 3. Accept the Let's Encrypt Terms of Service and click Save.

Nginx Proxy Manager will contact Let's Encrypt, retrieve a valid SSL certificate, configure Nginx, and reload the settings automatically.

docs.title: 5. Local Network Routing (DNS)
docs.text:
To access vault.local from other devices on your home network, those devices must know that vault.local points to your Raspberry Pi's IP address.

Since you are running Pi-hole, this is extremely easy to configure: 1. Access the Pi-hole admin interface at http://<RASPBERRY_PI_IP>:80/admin (or route it through NPM first). 2. Go to Local DNS $\rightarrow$ DNS Records. 3. Domain: Enter vault.local. 4. IP Address: Enter your Raspberry Pi's local IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.100). 5. Click Add.

Now, configure your router or local devices to use your Raspberry Pi's IP address as their primary DNS server.

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text:
• Setting Up Pi-hole on Docker Compose — Expanding DNS ad-blocking features.
  • Security Hardening — Secure Docker containers and firewall rules.

docs.title: Self-Hosted Local AI NVR with Frigate and Google Coral on Raspberry Pi
Self-Hosted Local AI NVR with Frigate and Google Coral on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
Most commercial home security cameras rely heavily on the cloud. This incurs monthly subscription costs, introduces high latency, and uploads your private video feeds to third-party servers.

Frigate is an open-source, local Network Video Recorder (NVR) that uses real-time AI object detection (powered by Google Coral) to analyze your camera streams locally. It only records and triggers alerts when actual objects (like people, cars, or dogs) are detected, ignoring wind, shadows, or rain.

This guide walks you through setting up Frigate with a Google Coral USB Accelerator on a Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: 1. Hardware Requirements
docs.text: To run real-time object detection on multiple high-definition camera feeds without melting your CPU, you need: - Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (4GB or 8GB RAM is highly recommended). - Google Coral USB Accelerator (essential for offloading AI tensor computations. Running YOLO/MobileNet models on the Pi's CPU directly is too slow and will peg CPU cores at 100%). - USB 3.0 connection (the Coral must be plugged into one of the Pi's blue USB 3.0 ports to prevent bandwidth bottlenecks). - Active Cooling (the Raspberry Pi and Google Coral will run hot during continuous video decoding and inference loops).

docs.title: 2. Docker Compose Configuration
docs.text:
We will deploy Frigate inside a Docker container. Create a dedicated directory structure:

mkdir -p ~/frigate/config ~/frigate/storage
cd ~/frigate
nano docker-compose.yml

docs.title: docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
version: '3.8'

services:
  frigate:
    container_name: frigate
    privileged: true # Required for USB Coral access
    restart: unless-stopped
    image: ghcr.io/blakeblackshear/frigate:stable
    shm_size: "128mb" # Prevents frame rendering crashes
    devices:
      - /dev/bus/usb:/dev/bus/usb # Mount USB bus for Google Coral
      - /dev/dri/renderD128:/dev/dri/renderD128 # Mount GPU for HW decoding
    volumes:
      - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro
      - ./config:/config
      - ./storage:/media/frigate
    ports:
      - "5000:5000" # Web UI port
      - "8554:8554" # RTSP feed re-stream port
    environment:
      - FRIGATE_RTSP_PASSWORD=ChooseSecurePassword

docs.title: 3. Configuring Frigate (config.yml)
docs.text:
Frigate requires a configuration file named config.yml inside the ./config directory to define detector hardware, camera inputs, and active zones.

nano config/config.yml

docs.title: config.yml
docs.text:
# 1. Define Object Detectors
detectors:
  coral:
    type: edgetpu
    device: usb

# 2. Global settings
mqtt:
  enabled: false # Optional: connect to Home Assistant later

# 3. Define Cameras
cameras:
  front_door:
    enabled: true
    ffmpeg:
      # Feed URL from your IP Camera (RTSP format)
      inputs:
        - path: rtsp://admin:password@192.168.1.50:554/stream1
          roles:
            - detect
            - record
      # Optimize HW decoding using Raspberry Pi's GPU
      hwaccel_args: preset-rpi-64bit

    # 4. Configure Object Detection
    detect:
      enabled: true
      width: 1280
      height: 720
      fps: 5

    # 5. Define Objects of Interest
    objects:
      track:
        - person
        - dog
        - car

    # 6. Configure Local Recording
    record:
      enabled: true
      retain:
        days: 3
        mode: all # Record all video or only events
      events:
        retain:
          default: 10 # Retain object detection event clips for 10 days

docs.title: 4. Launching the Stack
docs.text:
Verify your Google Coral is detected by the Pi: 

lsusb
(You should see an entry for "Global Unichip Corp." or "Google Inc.").

Start the container: 

docker compose up -d

docs.title: 5. Using the Web Interface
docs.text:
Open your browser and navigate to http://<RASPBERRY_PI_IP>:5000.

  • Live View: Displays real-time camera streams with bounding boxes tracking objects (e.g. person: 84%).
  • Events: Shows recorded clips of detected events.
  • Debug: Shows system performance metrics (TPU temperature, system memory usage, and inference times in milliseconds). A typical Coral TPU will process images in 5ms - 15ms, whereas a Raspberry Pi CPU takes 100ms - 200ms.

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text:
• Self-Hosted Setup with Docker Compose — Secure routing for the NVR interface.
  • Security Hardening — Securing local video files and network streams.

docs.title: Setting Up Pi-hole and Unbound on Docker Compose for Network-Wide Ad Blocking
Setting Up Pi-hole and Unbound on Docker Compose for Network-Wide Ad Blocking
docs.text: Block advertising networks and tracking scripts network-wide while securing your DNS queries! This guide walks you through setting up Pi-hole alongside Unbound as a recursive DNS resolver using Docker Compose.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Pi-hole is a popular DNS sinkhole that blocks advertisements and tracking domains for all devices on your local network. However, by default, Pi-hole forwards DNS queries to upstream public servers (like Google or Cloudflare), allowing those companies to log your browsing history.

By pairing Pi-hole with Unbound, you create a private, recursive DNS resolver. Unbound communicates directly with root DNS authority servers, bypassing third-party upstream providers completely.

Running this setup inside Docker Compose keeps your configurations clean and isolated.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Raspberry Pi running Raspberry Pi OS.
  • Docker and Docker Compose installed.
    • If not installed, run: 
      curl -sSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# Log out and log back in to apply group changes

docs.title: Step 1: Resolve Port 53 Conflicts
docs.text:
By default, modern Linux systems run systemd-resolved, which binds to Port 53 (the standard DNS port). This will block Pi-hole from starting. You must disable this local listener.

  1. Disable systemd-resolved: 
    sudo systemctl stop systemd-resolved
sudo systemctl disable systemd-resolved
  2. Configure a static DNS resolver for the Raspberry Pi itself so it can still download Docker images: 
    sudo nano /etc/resolv.conf
    Replace the content with a public DNS server (e.g., Cloudflare): 
    nameserver 1.1.1.1

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Project Directories
docs.text:
Set up a directory structure to store your configuration files.

mkdir -p ~/pihole-unbound/pihole
mkdir -p ~/pihole-unbound/unbound
cd ~/pihole-unbound

Create a custom Unbound configuration file: 

nano unbound/unbound.conf

Paste the following secure recursive resolver configuration: 

server:
    verbosity: 1
    interface: 0.0.0.0@5335
    do-ip4: yes
    do-udp: yes
    do-tcp: yes

    # Allow queries from local network only
    access-control: 127.0.0.0/8 allow
    access-control: 172.16.0.0/12 allow
    access-control: 192.168.0.0/16 allow

    # Hide identity
    hide-identity: yes
    hide-version: yes

    # Security settings
    harden-glue: yes
    harden-dnssec-stripped: yes
    use-caps-for-id: no
    edns-buffer-size: 1232
    prefetch: yes
    num-threads: 1
Note: Unbound is configured to run on port 5335 to avoid conflicting with Pi-hole's port 53.

docs.title: Step 3: Write the Docker Compose File
docs.text:
Now create the docker-compose.yml file to link both containers.

nano docker-compose.yml

Add the following multi-container service definition: 

version: "3"

services:
  unbound:
    image: mvance/unbound:latest
    container_name: unbound
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./unbound:/opt/unbound/etc/unbound
    networks:
      private_net:
        ipv4_address: 172.20.0.2

  pihole:
    image: pihole/pihole:latest
    container_name: pihole
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "53:53/tcp"
      - "53:53/udp"
      - "80:80/tcp"
    environment:
      TZ: 'UTC'
      WEBPASSWORD: 'your_secure_password_here' # Change this password!
      PIHOLE_DNS_: '172.20.0.2#5335'
    volumes:
      - ./pihole/etc-pihole:/etc/pihole
      - ./pihole/etc-dnsmasq.d:/etc/dnsmasq.d
    depends_on:
      - unbound
    networks:
      private_net:
        ipv4_address: 172.20.0.3

networks:
  private_net:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.20.0.0/16

docs.title: Step 4: Build and Start the Services
docs.text:
Start the containers in detached (background) mode:

docker compose up -d

Verify that both containers are running: 

docker ps

docs.title: Accessing the Web Dashboard
docs.text: Open a web browser on your computer and navigate to http://your-pi-ip/admin. Log in using the password you set in the WEBPASSWORD field of the compose file.

docs.title: Step 5: Test DNS Resolving
docs.text:
To verify that Pi-hole is successfully routing DNS queries recursively through Unbound:

  1. Open your terminal on your PC and run: 
    nslookup pi-hole.net your-pi-ip
  2. In the Pi-hole dashboard, go to Settings > DNS. You should see that "Custom 1 (IPv4)" is checked and points to 172.20.0.2#5335 (our Unbound container).

docs.title: Step 6: Configure Your Router
docs.text: To apply ad blocking network-wide: 1. Log in to your home router's admin portal. 2. Find the LAN DNS Settings or DHCP Server Settings. 3. Set the Primary DNS Server IP to your Raspberry Pi's local static IP address. 4. Renew your devices' network connections (disconnect and reconnect Wi-Fi), and ads will be blocked on all phones, tablets, smart TVs, and computers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Containers fail to start (port 53 in use):
    • Double check if systemd-resolved was disabled properly by running sudo lsof -i :53. If another DNS server like dnsmasq is running, stop it with sudo systemctl stop dnsmasq.
  • DNS queries are failing (cannot access internet):
    • Verify container logs by running docker logs unbound and docker logs pihole to check for misconfigurations in the unbound rules.

docs.title: Setting up VPN Access
docs.text: This guide explains how to set up various VPN solutions on your Raspberry Pi, including both VPN server (hosting your own VPN) and VPN client (connecting to external VPN services) configurations.

docs.title: VPN Options Overview
docs.text:
There are several VPN solutions you can implement on Raspberry Pi:

  1. OpenVPN - Traditional, secure, and widely supported
  2. WireGuard - Modern, fast, and lightweight
  3. PiVPN - Simplified OpenVPN/WireGuard installer
  4. Commercial VPN clients - Connecting to services like NordVPN, ExpressVPN

docs.title: Option 1: Setting up WireGuard VPN Server
docs.text: WireGuard is the recommended modern VPN solution due to its simplicity and performance.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Update system
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install WireGuard
sudo apt install wireguard -y

docs.title: Generate Keys
docs.text:
# Navigate to WireGuard directory
cd /etc/wireguard

# Generate server private key
sudo wg genkey | sudo tee server_private.key

# Generate server public key
sudo cat server_private.key | wg pubkey | sudo tee server_public.key

# Generate client private key
sudo wg genkey | sudo tee client_private.key

# Generate client public key
sudo cat client_private.key | wg pubkey | sudo tee client_public.key

# Set proper permissions
sudo chmod 600 server_private.key client_private.key

docs.title: Server Configuration
docs.text:
Create the server configuration file:

sudo nano /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf

Add the following configuration:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY>
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820
PostUp = iptables -A FORWARD -i %i -j ACCEPT; iptables -A FORWARD -o %i -j ACCEPT; iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
PostDown = iptables -D FORWARD -i %i -j ACCEPT; iptables -D FORWARD -o %i -j ACCEPT; iptables -t nat -D POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE

[Peer]
PublicKey = <CLIENT_PUBLIC_KEY>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32

Replace <SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY> and <CLIENT_PUBLIC_KEY> with the generated keys.

docs.title: Enable IP Forwarding
docs.text:
# Enable IP forwarding
echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

# Apply changes
sudo sysctl -p

docs.title: Start WireGuard Service
docs.text:
# Enable and start WireGuard
sudo systemctl enable wg-quick@wg0
sudo systemctl start wg-quick@wg0

# Check status
sudo systemctl status wg-quick@wg0

docs.title: Client Configuration
docs.text:
Create a client configuration file:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <CLIENT_PRIVATE_KEY>
Address = 10.0.0.2/24
DNS = 8.8.8.8

[Peer]
PublicKey = <SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY>
Endpoint = <YOUR_PI_PUBLIC_IP>:51820
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0
PersistentKeepalive = 25

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
# Allow WireGuard port through firewall
sudo ufw allow 51820/udp

# Enable UFW if not already enabled
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: Option 2: Using PiVPN (Automated Setup)
docs.text: PiVPN provides an easy installation script for both OpenVPN and WireGuard.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Download and run PiVPN installer
curl -L https://install.pivpn.io | bash

Follow the interactive installer: 1. Choose your VPN protocol (WireGuard recommended) 2. Configure network settings 3. Set up port forwarding 4. Create certificates/keys

docs.title: Adding Clients
docs.text:
# Add a new client
pivpn add

# List clients
pivpn list

# Generate QR code for mobile devices
pivpn -qr <client_name>

# Remove a client
pivpn revoke

docs.title: Managing PiVPN
docs.text:
# Check status
pivpn status

# Restart service
sudo systemctl restart wg-quick@wg0  # For WireGuard
# or
sudo systemctl restart openvpn@server  # For OpenVPN

# View logs
journalctl -u wg-quick@wg0 -f

docs.title: Option 3: OpenVPN Server Setup
docs.text: If you prefer OpenVPN over WireGuard:

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Install OpenVPN and Easy-RSA
sudo apt install openvpn easy-rsa -y

# Copy Easy-RSA templates
sudo cp -r /usr/share/easy-rsa /etc/openvpn/

docs.title: Certificate Authority Setup
docs.text:
cd /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa
sudo ./easyrsa init-pki
sudo ./easyrsa build-ca

# Generate server certificate
sudo ./easyrsa gen-req server nopass
sudo ./easyrsa sign-req server server

# Generate Diffie-Hellman parameters
sudo ./easyrsa gen-dh

# Generate TLS authentication key
sudo openvpn --genkey --secret ta.key

docs.title: Server Configuration
docs.text:
Create /etc/openvpn/server.conf:

sudo nano /etc/openvpn/server.conf

port 1194
proto udp
dev tun
ca /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa/pki/ca.crt
cert /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa/pki/issued/server.crt
key /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa/pki/private/server.key
dh /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa/pki/dh.pem
tls-auth /etc/openvpn/easy-rsa/ta.key 0

server 10.8.0.0 255.255.255.0
ifconfig-pool-persist ipp.txt

push "redirect-gateway def1 bypass-dhcp"
push "dhcp-option DNS 8.8.8.8"
push "dhcp-option DNS 8.8.4.4"

keepalive 10 120
cipher AES-256-CBC
user nobody
group nogroup
persist-key
persist-tun

status openvpn-status.log
log-append /var/log/openvpn.log
verb 3

docs.title: Option 4: VPN Client Setup
docs.text: To connect your Raspberry Pi to commercial VPN services:

docs.title: OpenVPN Client
docs.text:
# Install OpenVPN client
sudo apt install openvpn -y

# Download your VPN provider's configuration files
# Example for NordVPN:
cd /etc/openvpn
sudo wget https://downloads.nordcdn.com/configs/archives/servers/ovpn.zip
sudo unzip ovpn.zip

Create credentials file:

sudo nano /etc/openvpn/auth.txt

your_username
your_password

sudo chmod 600 /etc/openvpn/auth.txt

Connect to VPN:

# Connect to specific server
sudo openvpn --config /etc/openvpn/ovpn_udp/us1234.nordvpn.com.udp.ovpn --auth-user-pass /etc/openvpn/auth.txt

# Or set up as service
sudo systemctl enable openvpn@us1234.nordvpn.com.udp
sudo systemctl start openvpn@us1234.nordvpn.com.udp

docs.title: WireGuard Client
docs.text:
For WireGuard-based VPN services:

# Create client configuration
sudo nano /etc/wireguard/client.conf

Add your provider's configuration, then:

# Connect
sudo wg-quick up client

# Disconnect
sudo wg-quick down client

# Auto-start on boot
sudo systemctl enable wg-quick@client

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Configure your router to forward VPN traffic:

  • WireGuard: Forward UDP port 51820
  • OpenVPN: Forward UDP port 1194 (or your chosen port)

docs.title: Dynamic DNS Setup
docs.text:
If you don't have a static IP:

# Install ddclient for dynamic DNS
sudo apt install ddclient -y

# Configure ddclient
sudo nano /etc/ddclient.conf

Example configuration for No-IP:

protocol=noip
use=web
web=checkip.dyndns.org
server=dynupdate.no-ip.com
login=your_username
password='your_password'
your_hostname.ddns.net

docs.title: Firewall Rules
docs.text:
# Allow only VPN traffic and SSH
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow ssh
sudo ufw allow 51820/udp  # WireGuard
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: Key Management
docs.text:
# Backup your keys securely
sudo tar -czf wireguard_backup.tar.gz /etc/wireguard/
# Store this backup in a secure location

# Regular key rotation (recommended every 6 months)
# Generate new keys and update configurations

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
# Monitor VPN connections
sudo wg show

# Check logs
sudo journalctl -u wg-quick@wg0 -f

# Monitor network traffic
sudo iftop -i wg0

docs.title: CPU Governor Settings
docs.text:
# Set performance governor for better VPN throughput
echo 'performance' | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor

docs.title: Network Buffer Tuning
docs.text:
Add to /etc/sysctl.conf:

# Increase network buffers for VPN
net.core.rmem_default = 262144
net.core.rmem_max = 16777216
net.core.wmem_default = 262144
net.core.wmem_max = 16777216

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. Can't connect from outside network

    • Check port forwarding on router
    • Verify firewall rules
    • Confirm public IP address

  2. Slow VPN performance

    • Try different ciphers/protocols
    • Check CPU usage
    • Optimize network settings

  3. DNS not working through VPN

    • Check DNS settings in VPN config
    • Test with nslookup through VPN

docs.title: Diagnostic Commands
docs.text:
# Check VPN interface
ip addr show wg0

# Test connectivity
ping 8.8.8.8

# Check routing table
ip route

# Monitor VPN traffic
sudo tcpdump -i wg0

# Check if VPN is working
curl ipinfo.io/ip

docs.title: Log Analysis
docs.text:
# WireGuard logs
sudo journalctl -u wg-quick@wg0

# OpenVPN logs
sudo tail -f /var/log/openvpn.log

# System logs
sudo dmesg | grep -i vpn

docs.title: Split Tunneling
docs.text:
Configure selective routing through VPN:

# Create custom routing table
echo "200 vpn" | sudo tee -a /etc/iproute2/rt_tables

# Add routes for specific subnets only
sudo ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 dev wg0 table vpn
sudo ip rule add from 192.168.1.0/24 table vpn

docs.title: Kill Switch
docs.text:
Prevent traffic when VPN is down:

# Block all traffic except VPN
sudo iptables -I OUTPUT ! -o wg0 -m mark ! --mark $(wg show wg0 fwmark) -m addrtype ! --dst-type LOCAL -j REJECT

docs.title: Multi-Client Setup
docs.text:
For multiple simultaneous connections:

# In server config, add multiple peer sections
[Peer]
PublicKey = <CLIENT1_PUBLIC_KEY>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32

[Peer]
PublicKey = <CLIENT2_PUBLIC_KEY>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.3/32

docs.title: Automated Monitoring Script
docs.text:
Create /home/pi/vpn_monitor.sh:

#!/bin/bash
# Check if VPN is running and restart if needed

if ! systemctl is-active --quiet wg-quick@wg0; then
    echo "$(date): VPN down, restarting..." >> /var/log/vpn_monitor.log
    systemctl start wg-quick@wg0
fi

# Log connected clients
echo "$(date): $(wg show wg0 peers | wc -l) clients connected" >> /var/log/vpn_stats.log

# Make executable
chmod +x /home/pi/vpn_monitor.sh

# Add to crontab for regular monitoring
echo "*/5 * * * * /home/pi/vpn_monitor.sh" | crontab -

docs.title: Usage Statistics
docs.text:
# Get transfer statistics
sudo wg show wg0 transfer

# Monitor bandwidth usage
sudo vnstat -i wg0

docs.title: Taking It Further
docs.text:
• Set up a VPN dashboard with web interface
  • Implement automatic client provisioning
  • Create mobile apps for easy connection
  • Set up site-to-site VPN connections
  • Integrate with home automation systems

This comprehensive VPN setup enables secure remote access to your home network and protects your internet traffic when using public networks.

docs.title: Static IP Configuration on Raspberry Pi OS
Static IP Configuration on Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text: Setting a static IP address ensures your Raspberry Pi always uses the same network address, which is essential for servers, remote access, and IoT deployments. This guide covers all methods for configuring static IPs on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and later.

docs.title: Why Use a Static IP?
docs.text:
By default, your Raspberry Pi gets a dynamic IP via DHCP from your router. This IP can change after reboots or lease expirations, which causes problems when:

  • SSH / VNC access — You need a consistent address to connect to
  • Running servers — Web servers, Pi-hole, Home Assistant need a fixed address
  • Port forwarding — Router rules point to a specific IP
  • IoT devices — Other devices on your network need to find your Pi reliably
  • DNS records — Internal DNS entries need a stable target

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before configuring a static IP, gather your network information:

# Check your current IP, gateway, and DNS
ip addr show
ip route show default
cat /etc/resolv.conf

Note these values:

Parameter Example How to Find Current IP 192.168.1.50 ip addr show eth0 Subnet Mask /24 (255.255.255.0) Same as above Gateway 192.168.1.1 ip route show default DNS Servers 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1 cat /etc/resolv.conf Connection Name "Wired connection 1" nmcli connection show

Avoid IP conflicts

Choose an IP address outside your router's DHCP range. Most routers use DHCP range 192.168.1.100–200, so picking an address like 192.168.1.10–50 is usually safe. Check your router's admin page to confirm.

docs.title: Method 1: NetworkManager (nmcli) — Recommended
docs.text: Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (and later) uses NetworkManager as the default network manager. This is the recommended method.

docs.title: Configuring Ethernet (Wired)
docs.text:
# Step 1: Check your connection name
nmcli connection show

You'll see output like:

NAME                UUID                                  TYPE      DEVICE
Wired connection 1  a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890  ethernet  eth0
preconfigured       f1e2d3c4-b5a6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890  wifi      wlan0

# Step 2: Set static IP, gateway, and DNS
sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
  ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1" \
  ipv4.method manual

# Step 3: Apply changes
sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

docs.title: Configuring Wi-Fi (Wireless)
docs.text:
# Step 1: Find your Wi-Fi connection name
nmcli connection show

# Step 2: Set static IP for Wi-Fi
sudo nmcli connection modify "preconfigured" \
  ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.101/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1" \
  ipv4.method manual

# Step 3: Apply changes
sudo nmcli connection up "preconfigured"

docs.title: Reverting to DHCP
docs.text:
If you need to go back to automatic IP assignment:

sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
  ipv4.addresses "" \
  ipv4.gateway "" \
  ipv4.dns "" \
  ipv4.method auto

sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

docs.title: Method 2: nmtui — Interactive Text UI
docs.text:
If you prefer a visual interface in the terminal:

sudo nmtui
  1. Select Edit a connection
  2. Choose your connection (e.g., "Wired connection 1")
  3. Change IPv4 CONFIGURATION from Automatic to Manual
  4. Click Add next to Addresses and enter your static IP (e.g., 192.168.1.100/24)
  5. Set the Gateway (e.g., 192.168.1.1)
  6. Add DNS servers (e.g., 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1)
  7. Click OK → Back → Quit
  8. Restart the connection:
sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

docs.title: Method 3: dhcpcd.conf — Legacy Method
docs.text:
For older Raspberry Pi OS versions only

This method works on Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye and earlier, which use dhcpcd instead of NetworkManager. If you're on Bookworm or later, use Method 1.

Edit /etc/dhcpcd.conf:

sudo nano /etc/dhcpcd.conf

Add at the end of the file:

# Static IP for Ethernet
interface eth0
static ip_address=192.168.1.100/24
static routers=192.168.1.1
static domain_name_servers=8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1

# Static IP for Wi-Fi
interface wlan0
static ip_address=192.168.1.101/24
static routers=192.168.1.1
static domain_name_servers=8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1

Apply changes:

sudo systemctl restart dhcpcd

docs.title: Configuring IPv6 Static Address
docs.text:
To set a static IPv6 address alongside your IPv4 configuration:

# Set static IPv6 address
sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
  ipv6.addresses "fd00::100/64" \
  ipv6.gateway "fd00::1" \
  ipv6.method manual

# Apply
sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

To disable IPv6 entirely (useful for reducing attack surface on IoT devices):

sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
  ipv6.method disabled

sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

docs.title: Verifying Your Configuration
docs.text:
After applying changes, verify everything works:

# Check IP address
ip addr show eth0

# Check gateway/routing
ip route show default

# Check DNS resolution
nslookup google.com

# Test internet connectivity
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
ping -c 4 google.com

# Check NetworkManager connection details
nmcli connection show "Wired connection 1" | grep ipv4

docs.title: Advanced: DHCP Reservation (Alternative Approach)
docs.text:
Instead of configuring a static IP on the Pi itself, you can reserve an IP in your router's DHCP settings. This way, the Pi still uses DHCP but always gets the same IP.

Advantages:

  • No configuration changes on the Pi
  • Centralized IP management on the router
  • Works even after OS reinstall

How to set up:

  1. Log into your router's admin page (usually 192.168.1.1)
  2. Find DHCP Reservation or Address Reservation (varies by router)
  3. Add your Pi's MAC address and desired IP
  4. Save and restart the Pi

Find your Pi's MAC address:

ip link show eth0 | grep ether
# Example output: link/ether dc:a6:32:xx:xx:xx

docs.title: "No internet after setting static IP"
docs.text:
Cause: Incorrect gateway or DNS settings.

# Check if gateway is reachable
ping -c 2 192.168.1.1

# If gateway works but DNS doesn't:
ping -c 2 8.8.8.8        # Works → DNS problem
nslookup google.com       # Fails → Confirm DNS issue

# Fix DNS
sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
  ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1"
sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

docs.title: "IP address conflict detected"
docs.text:
Cause: Another device on your network already uses the same IP.

# Scan for IP conflicts
sudo apt install arp-scan
sudo arp-scan --localnet | grep 192.168.1.100

Choose a different IP that's not in use.

docs.title: "Static IP works but reverts after reboot"
docs.text:
Cause: Multiple network managers are conflicting.

# Check which network manager is active
systemctl status NetworkManager
systemctl status dhcpcd

# On Bookworm, ensure dhcpcd is disabled
sudo systemctl disable dhcpcd
sudo systemctl stop dhcpcd

docs.title: "Cannot SSH after changing IP"
docs.text:
Cause: You're trying to connect to the old IP.

# From another machine, find the Pi's new IP:
# Option 1: Check your router's connected devices list
# Option 2: Scan the network
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 | grep -B 2 "Raspberry"
# Option 3: If you have mDNS working
ping raspberrypi.local

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Document your IP assignments — Keep a spreadsheet or document listing all static IPs on your network
  2. Use IPs outside the DHCP range — Prevents conflicts with automatically assigned addresses
  3. Always set a DNS server — Without DNS, you can reach IPs but not domain names
  4. Test connectivity after changes — Always verify with ping before closing your SSH session
  5. Have physical access as backup — If you lose network access, you'll need a keyboard and monitor
  6. Consider DHCP reservation — Often easier and more maintainable than static configuration

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text:
• Networking Setup and Management — Complete networking guide
  • Headless Setup Guide — Set up your Pi without a monitor
  • Security Hardening Guide — Secure your network-connected Pi
  • Tailscale Remote Access — Access your Pi from anywhere without port forwarding

docs.title: Storage Optimization: Btrfs File System with Transparent Compression and Snapshots on Raspberry Pi
Storage Optimization: Btrfs File System with Transparent Compression and Snapshots on Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
The default file system for Raspberry Pi OS is ext4. While ext4 is stable and widely supported, it is a traditional file system that lacks modern storage features. Raspberry Pi devices rely heavily on microSD cards, which have limited write cycles and slower raw read/write speeds compared to SSDs. If the power is abruptly cut to a running Pi, ext4 partitions can occasionally suffer from file system corruption.

By migrating your storage partitions to Btrfs (B-tree File System), you unlock advanced storage capabilities directly on the Pi: - Transparent Compression: Data is compressed on-the-fly (using zstd or lzo) before being written to disk, reducing SD card wear and saving storage space. - Copy-on-Write (CoW) Snapshots: Instantly back up your entire operating system or configuration directories with zero initial storage overhead. - Self-Healing: Btrfs uses checksums for metadata and data, allowing it to detect silent data corruption.

This guide provides a comprehensive tutorial for setting up Btrfs, formatting partitions, configuring transparent zstd compression, managing subvolumes, and automating snapshots to protect your home server from corruption.

docs.title: 1. How Btrfs Optimizes SD Cards
docs.text:
In a traditional file system, when a file is modified, the data is overwritten directly in place. If the system loses power during this write window, the file is corrupted.

graph TD subgraph ext4 (In-place Write) A[Original Data block] -->|Overwrite| B[Corrupted block on Power Cut] end subgraph Btrfs (Copy-on-Write) C[Original Data block] -->|Modify| D[Write modified data to free space] D -->|Update pointer| E[New Metadata pointing to new block] end

Under Copy-on-Write, Btrfs writes modified data to a completely new, free location on the storage media. Only after the write operation completes successfully does the file system update its metadata pointers to point to the new data. If the power drops mid-write, the pointers still point to the safe, original data, preventing corruption.

Furthermore, Transparent Compression means that when an application writes 100MB of text or code, Btrfs compresses it (e.g., to 30MB) in CPU RAM and writes only 30MB to the physical SD card. Because writing to flash storage is slow and wears out memory cells, reducing physical writes directly extends the life of your SD card and improves write throughput.

docs.title: 2. Installing Utilities and Mounting a Secondary Disk
docs.text: Before converting your primary boot partition, it is highly recommended to practice Btrfs operations using a secondary USB flash drive or external SSD.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Btrfs Tools
docs.text:
First, install the user-space management tools: 

sudo apt update
sudo apt install btrfs-progs -y

docs.title: Step 2: Identify the Disk Partition
docs.text:
Plug in your USB storage drive and identify its device identifier: 

lsblk
You will see output similar to this: 
NAME        MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda           8:0    0  28.9G  0 disk 
└─sda1        8:1    0  28.9G  0 part 
mmcblk0     179:0    0  59.5G  0 disk 
├─mmcblk0p1 179:1    0   512M  0 part /boot/firmware
└─mmcblk0p2 179:2    0    59G  0 part /
In this example, the secondary USB partition is /dev/sda1.

docs.title: Step 3: Format the Partition with Btrfs
docs.text:
Format the device partition: 

# WARNING: This deletes all data on the target partition!
sudo mkfs.btrfs -f /dev/sda1
The output displays the UUID and default block parameters: 
btrfs-progs v6.1.2
See https://btrfs.wiki.kernel.org for more information.

Label:              (null)
UUID:               a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
Node size:          16384
Sector size:        4096
Filesystem size:    28.90GiB

docs.title: 3. Subvolumes and Mount Options for SD Card Optimization
docs.text: Btrfs uses the concept of Subvolumes. A subvolume is a named, mountable directory tree within the filesystem, but unlike a partition, it shares the free space of the entire pool.

docs.title: Step 1: Mount the Root Btrfs Directory
docs.text:
Create a temporary mount point and mount the root of the filesystem: 

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/btrfs-root
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/btrfs-root
